techniques.name: Category Dismissal Then Redirect
techniques.lede: Write off a whole category in a few blunt words, then hand the reader the thing they should want instead.
techniques.what_it_does: A short, flat verdict condemns an entire class of products, advice, or habits ("most of this is junk"), and before the reader can argue, the copy names the better option. The dismissal does the attention work: it sounds like a friend telling the plain truth, not a sales pitch. The redirect turns that jolt into direction. No case is built and no single rival is debated; the category is simply waved off, and the alternative steps into the gap the dismissal just opened.
techniques.why_it_works: Bluntness reads as honesty. A curt verdict signals the speaker is not managing your impression, which lowers the guard and buys belief. It also does the reader's sorting for them: a crowded, confusing field collapses into "that is junk, this is the answer," which feels like relief. The dismissal opens a small loop, so what should I use, and the immediate redirect closes it before doubt can set in. Naming the enemy category also flatters the reader as someone too sharp for it, and pulls them onto the speaker's side.
techniques.lands_when: The dismissal is short and flat, a verdict rather than an argument.; The category being written off is one the reader already half-distrusts.; The alternative arrives immediately, so the opened doubt closes fast.; The speaker sounds like a candid insider, not a rival vendor pitching.
techniques.dilutes_when: The dismissal swells into a long reasoned case, which reads as contrarian argument instead.; No clear alternative follows, leaving only a complaint hanging.; The condemned category is vague, so nothing concrete actually gets rejected.; The tone tips into insult before the reader has any reason to trust the speaker.

techniques.name: Quick Quiz
techniques.lede: A short battery of self-assessment questions, or an open invitation to take a quiz, that gets the reader to diagnose themselves before anyone tries to sell them anything.
techniques.what_it_does: It hands the reader a set of questions to answer about their own life, body, or business, or simply invites them to take a quiz. Each question, or the quiz itself, pulls the reader into silently checking their own experience against it, whether the answer is a yes or no or something more specific. The frame flips: instead of a pitch coming at them, the reader feels measured, tested, or sorted. By the time the reader finishes answering, or agrees to find out, they have built their own case for the problem, so the product arrives as a fitting answer rather than an interruption.
techniques.why_it_works: Answering questions about yourself is nearly automatic, so the reader engages before deciding whether to. Each yes is a small private admission that the problem is real and personal, and admissions made to yourself feel truer than claims made by a seller. The quiz frame also reverses status: the reader is being assessed, which signals that not everyone qualifies and that the answer will be tailored. Self-diagnosis carries more conviction than any outside assertion, so the reader walks toward the conclusion the copy wanted, believing they reached it themselves.
techniques.lands_when: The questions target felt symptoms or situations the reader recognizes instantly, so each one earns a silent yes; The frame positions the reader as being evaluated or sorted, not pitched, which lowers sales resistance; The quiz feels quick and low-effort, so starting it costs the reader almost nothing; Each answer deepens involvement and sets up the product as the natural payoff of the reader's o…
techniques.dilutes_when: The copy is really an enumerated list of warnings, foods, or mistakes with no questions for the reader to answer; Only one vague question is posed, so there is no real self-assessment, just a hook; The questions are so generic that any reader answers yes, draining the diagnosis of meaning; The quiz invitation is buried behind a flat label or CTA with no sense of being measured or qualified

techniques.name: Contrarian Data Point
techniques.lede: State a figure that collides with something the reader already believes, and leave the collision unexplained.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy states a number, a study result, or a measured outcome that collides head on with a belief the reader holds about their own field. The figure stands on its own, sometimes right after a quick naming of the assumption it is about to break, but it is not attached to a product pitch or a promise. The explanation for the figure does not arrive yet. The reader is left holding a contradiction between the number in front of them and the assumption behind them, and the only way to settle it is to keep reading.
techniques.why_it_works: A belief the reader has never had to defend feels like knowledge rather than opinion. A hard figure that cuts against it cannot be waved off the way a bare opinion can, so the reader has to reconcile the two, and reconciling takes attention. That attention is the sale. The move also converts the writer from a seller into a source, because someone handing over an uncomfortable number reads as someone reporting rather than pitching. The withheld explanation keeps the tension open long enough for the argument that follows to land inside it.
techniques.lands_when: The belief being contradicted is one the reader genuinely holds and has never questioned; The figure is specific and checkable, so it reads as a finding rather than a boast; The explanation is withheld for a beat, leaving the contradiction standing on its own; What follows actually resolves the number, so the opening is a door and not a stunt
techniques.dilutes_when: The statistic is merely surprising and does not cut against anything the reader believes; The number is round, hedged, or unsourced, so it reads as a made up figure; The copy explains the figure in the same breath, closing the tension before it can pull; The claim is so extreme the reader rejects the source instead of the belief

techniques.name: Visual Typographic Interrupt
techniques.lede: Copy that breaks its own visual rules, bending letters, spacing, casing, or symbols so the eye trips a beat before the reader has finished reading.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy does something to its own surface rather than to its argument. Letters get stretched or swapped, a word gets cut across a line, capitals arrive where they are not needed, or a symbol lands in the middle of an otherwise ordinary sentence. The words may still say something plain. The break sits in how they look. Sometimes the copy points at the oddity and tells the reader it was on purpose. The eye snags first, and the reading brain catches up after.
techniques.why_it_works: Reading runs on habit. Eyes move quickly over text that behaves the way text usually behaves, and much of a page gets skimmed rather than read. A shape that does not fit stops that glide, because something has to be sorted out before reading can carry on. The pause is short, but it costs attention the reader did not plan to spend, and whatever sits in that spot gets looked at closely instead of scanned. Because the oddity is visible before it is read, it can catch a reader who was only passing through.
techniques.lands_when: The break is short and rare, so it reads as a deliberate choice and not as the house style.; The odd spelling, casing, or symbol carries part of the meaning instead of only decorating it.; The copy around it is plain enough that there is a rhythm worth breaking.; The voice is already playful or blunt, so the trick sounds like the same speaker who wrote the rest.
techniques.dilutes_when: Every line shouts, so nothing on the page stands out from anything else.; The device is hung on a sentence that would say exactly the same thing without it.; The reader has to stop and work out what happened before any meaning arrives.; The tone of the trick fights the tone of the offer, which bites hardest in serious or high-trust categories.

techniques.name: Document Anchor Open
techniques.lede: Point the reader at a specific document, code, or object, and let its bare existence carry the claim.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy steers the reader's eye toward a concrete thing: a government code, a law section, a leaked memo, a photograph, a piece of official-looking paper. Instead of asserting the claim outright, it makes the reader look at an artifact that seems to prove the claim on its own. The item is chosen to feel real enough to read as investigative and specific enough to feel exclusive, as though the reader has just been handed something very few other people have ever been shown.
techniques.why_it_works: A named document reads as evidence rather than opinion, so the reader lowers the usual sales guard and slips into the posture of examining a record. Specificity does the persuading: a code number, a page reference, or an object shot up close signals that a real thing exists and could be checked, even when the reader never checks it. The instruction to look also breaks the scan, borrowing the pull of a courtroom exhibit. Being shown a document implies access, and access implies the reader now stands on the inside.
techniques.lands_when: The artifact is concrete and named, a specific code, section, or object rather than a vague reference to paperwork.; The reader is invited to look, examine, or read for themselves, which shifts them from buyer into investigator.; The document plausibly exists and could in principle be checked, giving the claim a verifiable feel.; The thing shown carries an air of restricted access, so seeing it r…
techniques.dilutes_when: The document is generic or unnamed, so it reads as a prop instead of real evidence.; The copy shouts the conclusion and forgets to make the reader actually look at the thing.; The artifact is plainly invented or so overblown that the investigative pose collapses into hype.; A number, not an object, is really doing the work, which turns the move into a statistics anchor wearing document costume.

techniques.name: Pseudo Editorial Persona
techniques.lede: Pseudo Editorial Persona signs an advertisement with a person, giving the copy a name, a role, and enough publication furniture that it reads as something a writer produced rather than something a company placed.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy attaches a human author to itself. A name appears, and with it a role that gives the name standing: an editor's title, a doctor's honorific, a list of books the writer is known for. Publication furniture often follows, a masthead, a date, a reading time, a stated claim of independence. The shapes vary, from a bare byline under a headline to a full front page of credentials. The effect is that the reader begins reading a piece rather than an offer.
techniques.why_it_works: People read articles and advertisements with different guards up. An article carries an author who can be named, questioned, and held to what they wrote, so a byline signals that a person has put a reputation behind the words. The persona also answers the question every claim raises, which is who says so, before the claim itself arrives. And the furniture is cheap. A name, a title, and a date cost nothing to set in type, while the trust they borrow took publications a century to build.
techniques.lands_when: The name comes with a role that covers the subject, so the person's standing matches the claim they are about to make.; The furniture agrees with itself: name, title, publication, and date all point at the same imagined desk.; The writing holds an editorial register, describing, comparing, or telling a story rather than pitching.; The persona sits on the first screen, so the reader assigns what f…
techniques.dilutes_when: The name arrives bare, with no role, outlet, or date behind it to give it any standing.; The stated role has nothing to do with the subject, so the credential covers none of the claim.; The voice slips into sales register a line or two in, and the byline stops matching the copy underneath it.; Independence is asserted loudly instead of shown, which reads as protesting too much.

techniques.name: Strange Fact
techniques.lede: State a surprising, checkable fact that seems to have nothing to do with the product, and the reader stays to find out why it matters.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy states a genuinely odd, verifiable piece of information: a natural fact, a forgotten historical detail, a number nobody expects. The fact stands on its own, with no visible sales intent, so the reader's guard stays down. Because the fact seems unconnected to any offer, a question forms on its own: why am I being told this? The copy then builds a bridge from the strange fact to the product, and the reader crosses it willingly because they want the answer.
techniques.why_it_works: People are wired to resolve gaps between what they know and what they just learned; a fact that contradicts expectation creates an itch that only reading further can scratch. A verifiable fact also feels like a gift rather than a pitch, so it earns attention that a claim about the product never could. And because the reader arrived at the product through their own curiosity instead of the seller's insistence, the eventual pitch inherits some of the fact's credibility. The reader feels informed first and sold to second.
techniques.lands_when: The fact is genuinely surprising, specific, and true, the kind a reader would repeat at dinner.; The audience is cold or skeptical, because the fact opens attention before any product is mentioned.; The bridge from the fact to the offer feels discovered rather than forced, so the fact turns out to be the reason the product matters.; The channel rewards a stopped scroll or an opened envelope, such…
techniques.dilutes_when: The fact is common knowledge or only mildly interesting, so no curiosity gap opens.; The connection to the product is strained, and the reader feels baited and tricked at the reveal.; The fact cannot survive a quick check, and one false detail poisons trust in everything after it.; The fact is so fascinating that the reader remembers the trivia and forgets the offer.

techniques.name: Negation Frame
techniques.lede: Negation Frame tells the reader what this is not, denying the obvious assumption before offering anything in its place.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy makes a denial. Instead of stating what the thing is, it names what the reader already expects and rejects it: not that category, not that method, nothing to do with the usual answer. The assumed frame is spoken out loud only to be knocked down. This clears the reader's default guess off the table and leaves an open question in its place. If it is not that, then what is it? The positive claim, when it comes, arrives after the denial has done its work.
techniques.why_it_works: A denial does two things at once. It interrupts the pattern, because a reader braced for a pitch instead hears a refusal, and that breaks the skim. And it opens a loop: naming what something is not leaves the mind reaching for what it is, and that gap pulls attention forward. The move also flatters the reader by assuming they are sharp enough to have guessed the ordinary answer, then rewarding them with something past it. By starting from the reader's own expectation, the copy feels like it is reading their mind before it sells them anything.
techniques.lands_when: The denied thing is exactly what the reader would assume, so the negation lands on a real expectation.; What it is not is stated first and plainly, before any positive claim competes for attention.; The denial opens a genuine question the copy then pays off, rather than a dead end.; The rejected category carries fatigue or baggage, so the reader is relieved to hear it dismissed.
techniques.dilutes_when: The negation is buried after the pitch has already landed, so it leads nothing.; It denies a feature or ingredient rather than the frame, which reads as a spec list.; Nothing fills the gap the denial opens, leaving confusion instead of curiosity.; The thing denied is a straw man no reader actually assumed, so the reversal has no charge.

examples.why: The copy defines its subject by what it refuses to be, stacking 'not a Mining Stock, ETF, or Bullion' so the reader mentally clears every obvious gold vehicle before a single positive claim lands. The rejection does the work, manufacturing intrigue from absen…

techniques.name: Cold Confession
techniques.lede: Cold Confession states, flatly and without softening, a true fact that hurts the speaker's own case.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy makes an admission against its own interest: a flaw in the product, a failure, a cost, a loss, something the seller would normally bury. It is delivered plainly, ahead of the claim or offer it sits with, so the reader meets the weakness before the pitch. The tone stays level, closer to a plain statement of fact than an apology or a plea. Nothing is walked back in the same breath. Everything that follows has to be read in the light of what was just given away.
techniques.why_it_works: Readers open an ad braced for one-sided praise, so a self-damaging line breaks the expected pattern and buys a moment of real attention. It also reads as a costly signal: a seller willing to say the bad part out loud is likelier telling the truth about the rest, and the reader lowers the guard. The admission gets in front of the doubt the reader was already forming, so the objection never has to be argued down. The coldness carries the weight. Pleading or self-pity turns the admission into a bid for sympathy, which the reader discounts.
techniques.lands_when: The admission is genuinely costly, naming a real flaw or failure the seller could easily have hidden; It comes first, before any claim, so the honesty frames everything that follows; The wording is plain and specific, not a humble-brag dressed up as a weakness; What gets confessed connects to the promise ahead, so the turn from candor to pitch feels earned
techniques.dilutes_when: The flaw is really a boast in disguise, like admitting you care too much or work too hard; The admission is vague or generic, so it costs the writer nothing to say it; Nothing follows from it, leaving a raw disclosure with no payoff or turn; Every message opens this way, so the move reads as a house formula rather than a real moment

techniques.name: Numbered Revelation Promise
techniques.lede: A precise count of insights, reasons, or steps is promised up front while the insights themselves stay just out of reach, so the number itself becomes the reason to keep reading.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy names an exact quantity of things worth knowing, five ways, three reasons, ten patterns, a single numbered secret, and then declines to hand them over. The count does two jobs at once. It makes the payoff feel finite and knowable, something a reader can picture finishing, while the withheld content opens a loop that only reading further will close. The promise is specific enough to feel real and incomplete enough to pull the reader toward the reveal.
techniques.why_it_works: A bare number implies the material has already been sorted and counted, which reads as competence and makes the payoff feel bounded rather than vague. The mind treats an enumerated set as a task with a finish line, so a reader commits to reaching the end. Odd or large counts suggest depth and thoroughness, while small ones suggest a clean shortcut. Because the items are named by quantity but not by content, the reader carries an open question forward, and closing that question becomes reason enough to read on, click, or buy.
techniques.lands_when: The number is exact and the promised items stay withheld, so the count opens a loop rather than closing one.; The quantity fits the promise: a small count reads as a clean shortcut, a large one as uncommon depth.; The subject genuinely matters to the reader, so a finite list of answers feels worth finishing.; A single pointer such as 'the third reason' or 'Secret #2' singles out one item as the o…
techniques.dilutes_when: The list is fully delivered in the same breath, leaving nothing to pull the reader forward.; The number measures a claim or counts customers instead of naming withheld revelations.; The count is vague or hedged, such as 'a few' or 'up to ten', losing the exactness that signals sorted, finished material.; The promised items sound dull or generic, so the reader has no reason to spend attention clos…

techniques.name: The Pointed Question
techniques.lede: Ask a direct question pointed straight at the reader's own situation, and you make them answer before they can look away.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy puts a question to the reader about their current problem, fear, or wish. Instead of announcing a claim, it hands the reader a prompt they cannot help but answer in their own head. That silent answer pulls them one step into the message and frames everything that follows as a reply to a question they have already started thinking about. The question does the work of stopping the eye, naming the topic, and starting a small conversation, all in a single line.
techniques.why_it_works: A question creates an open loop the mind rushes to close. Reading one triggers an automatic, involuntary attempt to answer, so the reader is participating rather than being talked at. A well-aimed question also mirrors the reader's situation, which signals the writer understands them and earns a moment more attention. Because the reader supplies the answer themselves, the conclusion feels self-generated rather than imposed, and self-generated conclusions are stickier and less resisted. The opening question converts a passive scanner into an active respondent before any selling begins.
techniques.lands_when: The question targets a real problem, fear, or desire the reader already carries, so it feels aimed at them personally; It opens the copy and sets the frame, rather than arriving after the pitch is already made; The reader's own answer pulls them toward the offer, so engaging with the question is the first step toward acting; It is specific enough that the reader pictures their own case, not a vag…
techniques.dilutes_when: The answer is so obvious the question reads as throat-clearing and provokes no real thought; It asks about the brand or product instead of the reader, so the reader has no personal stake in answering; Several questions stack up front and no single one carries the load, scattering attention; The question is generic enough that any reader can answer no and keep scrolling

techniques.name: Confessional Secret-Habit Reveal
techniques.lede: A writer owns up to a private habit and then, in the very next line, says exactly what that habit is.
techniques.what_it_does: Two beats, back to back. The first names a habit as secret, odd, or slightly embarrassing, often with a note of regret that the writer did not start it sooner. The second says exactly what the habit is, in plain physical terms: the object, the moment, the small action. Question and answer sit in the same passage, so nothing is held back for a later paragraph or a click. The confession frame keeps the stakes low, since this is something the writer does quietly rather than advice handed down.
techniques.why_it_works: People lean in for secrets in a way they never lean in for claims, so the admission buys attention cheaply. Paying that attention back within a sentence is what separates the move from a tease: the reader gets the goods, and the writer reads as someone who does not withhold. Because the revealed action is small and physical, it can be pictured and copied tonight, with no change of identity required. A habit done in private also has no audience, so there is nothing to perform and nothing to fail at.
techniques.lands_when: The revealed action is small, physical, and repeatable, close enough for a reader to copy the same day.; The admission costs the writer something real: mild embarrassment, lateness, or a habit that sounds strange said out loud.; The reveal arrives immediately, in the same breath, with no part of the payoff saved for a click.; The voice is first person and concrete, naming the place, the object, o…
techniques.dilutes_when: The habit is named as secret but never actually revealed, which collapses the move into an ordinary teaser.; The confession is about a feeling or a character flaw rather than something the writer physically does.; The revealed behavior turns out to be a product pitch wearing the costume of a habit.; The admission carries no cost or risk, so the word secret reads as decoration instead of disclosur…

examples.excerpt: A business newsletter opener admitting to an early bedtime and linking it to how the company was built.
examples.why: The writer frames a private routine as an admission rather than advice, announcing 'a confession that might shock you' before disclosing that 'I go to bed at 9 PM like it's a religion.' The disclosure carries no instruction and no offer, only the habit itself…

techniques.name: Latent Value Reveal
techniques.lede: Tells the reader that something worth having is already theirs, sitting unnoticed, so the copy only has to point at it.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy names something of value the reader already owns, already qualifies for, or is already owed, then explains why it has gone unnoticed. Nothing new is promised at first. The reader's own account, property, records, customer base, or legal standing becomes the subject of the sentence. The product arrives afterward as the way to reach what is already sitting there, so the pitch reads as a discovery about the reader's own situation rather than as an offer being made to them.
techniques.why_it_works: People guard what they believe is already theirs far harder than they chase something new. Once the copy says the money, the right, or the asset exists under the reader's name, sitting still starts to feel like losing rather than like passing on a deal. It also lowers the guard that a promise raises, because the claim is about the reader's present, which they can go and check, not about a future the seller controls. And it opens a question the reader cannot answer alone: what do I hold that I have never counted?
techniques.lands_when: The thing named is real and checkable, something the reader can look up under their own name or find in their own records.; The reason it went unnoticed is given plainly, so being unaware reads as normal rather than careless.; The size of what is sitting there is stated in specific terms instead of being called potential.; The step from knowing to collecting is short, and the product is that step…
techniques.dilutes_when: What the reader supposedly already owns turns out to be a new purchase in disguise, and the whole frame reads as a trick.; The claim stays abstract, such as untapped potential or hidden power, with no asset actually named.; The wording scolds the reader for missing it, which turns a piece of good news into an accusation.; It is stacked with other loud claims, so the quiet fact about the reader's…

examples.excerpt: Page for a consumer legal app that walks people through searching state databases for unclaimed property.

examples.excerpt: Direct mail letter promoting a retirement finance guide to older savers.
examples.why: The copy locates the payoff inside the reader's existing situation rather than in something new to acquire: 'money you didn't even know you had' puts the asset already in hand and casts the offer as sight rather than purchase, while 'little-known strategies'…

examples.headline: Today, you have the data available to make informed business decisions, but it’s locked in your systems.
examples.excerpt: Site copy for sales intelligence software sold to dealer groups, describing what it does with data the buyer already collects.
examples.why: The copy hands the reader an asset already owned: 'you have the data available to make informed business decisions'. The value is stipulated as present and adequate, then stranded by one clause, 'locked in your systems'. The structural tell is the hinge on 'b…

techniques.name: Acknowledge-the-Trope Then Reassert
techniques.lede: Say the tired line out loud before the reader can, then keep going with the claim anyway.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy names the reaction the reader is already having: the line everyone repeats, the category that always disappoints, the label people pin on the brand. Naming it first costs the reader the small pleasure of thinking it first. What follows the admission varies: a claim that something has changed, an offer of proof, a counterclaim about the product, or a reframe that turns the label into a virtue. The admission usually sits early, at the point where the eye-roll would otherwise end the read.
techniques.why_it_works: A reader who has met the same pitch many times arrives with a dismissal already loaded. Copy that ignores it does not escape it; the reader supplies it silently and stops. Saying it first moves the objection out of the reader's head and into the writer's own words, which reads as honesty about the category rather than another push. It also shows the writer knows what the genre sounds like, so the next line is heard as a departure from it. The claim gets a second hearing it would not otherwise get.
techniques.lands_when: The audience has heard the claim so often that it has stopped registering.; The tired line is stated in the plain words a reader would actually use for it.; Something real follows the admission: a change, proof, or a specific counterclaim.; The admission stays short so the pivot arrives before the reader agrees with it.
techniques.dilutes_when: The acknowledgment runs longer than what answers it, so the copy argues itself out of the sale.; Nothing new backs the reassertion, leaving the reader holding only the objection.; The named trope is not one this reader was thinking, so the copy plants a doubt instead of clearing one.; Every section opens the same way, turning candor into a tic the reader learns to skip.

examples.why: The copy names the reader's objection before the reader can raise it: 'I know everyone says that' concedes that the claim is a worn one, and 'Most people started to tune it out' goes further, granting that the tuning out was reasonable. Having paid that price…

examples.excerpt: Opening line on the sales page for a plant-based meal shake.
examples.why: The copy names the objection the reader already holds before the reader can raise it. 'Let's be honest' flags the admission as candor, and 'taste like twigs and lawn clippings' states the category's reputation in the reader's own unflattering terms, spending…

techniques.name: Provocative Claims
techniques.lede: A bold, counter-intuitive, or deliberately affronting statement that seizes attention through the tension of disbelief.
techniques.what_it_does: It opens by asserting something the reader instinctively wants to argue with: a claim that contradicts settled wisdom, insults a comfortable assumption, inverts a familiar truth, or sounds too shocking to be true. The friction is the point. A reader who disagrees cannot simply move on; the mind snags on the gap between what it believes and what the line just stated, and reading forward becomes the only way to resolve the tension. The move buys attention with provocation rather than with a promised reward.
techniques.why_it_works: Belief runs on autopilot until something jars it. A statement that collides with what the reader holds true creates a small cognitive emergency, and the brain cannot ignore an open contradiction it has been handed. Curiosity and mild indignation both pull in the same direction: toward the next line, where the claim might be defended or dismantled. The provocation also signals a writer willing to say the unsafe thing, which reads as candor. Attention earned by friction is sticky, because the reader has already started arguing back in their own head.
techniques.lands_when: The claim genuinely contradicts something the reader believes or assumes, so the friction is real; The bold line is paid off by an argument that follows, not left as empty bluster; The provocation fits a voice the reader will accept as honest rather than merely rude; The statement is specific enough to feel like a real position, not a vague stir
techniques.dilutes_when: The line only promises a desirable outcome, so it reads as a big claim the reader wants rather than one they resist; The shock is gratuitous and unconnected to the offer, spending goodwill for no payoff; Every sentence strains to provoke, so the affront becomes background noise; The claim is so implausible it reads as a lie rather than a challenge worth weighing

examples.why: The line states a tactic that contradicts the reader's expectation of how selling works, asserting that you get people 'eager to buy' by 'refusing to sell to them.' The claim deliberately collides with common sense so the reader cannot let it pass unchallenge…

examples.excerpt: An airline ad dismisses a beloved proverb as outdated.
examples.why: The line takes a maxim everyone treats as settled wisdom and demotes it, naming the proverb only to strip its authority: 'Good things come to those who wait,' is just that: 'old.' The reduction to a single dismissive word does the work, converting received be…

techniques.name: Soft Pattern Interrupt
techniques.lede: A line that steps out of the expected tone or topic just far enough to make the reader notice, then hands the message straight back.
techniques.what_it_does: For a beat, the copy stops sounding like the copy around it. A joke lands where a fact was due, a piece of relationship wisdom turns toward an unlikely product, the writer stops to talk to the reader instead of about the offer, a question denies that the product is even there, or a scene turns out to mean something other than it first appeared. The break is small and it resolves quickly, and the surrounding message usually picks up again within a sentence or two.
techniques.why_it_works: Reading is prediction. A few lines into a newsletter, a product page, or an ad, the reader has guessed the shape of the rest and starts skimming to confirm the guess. A line that does not fit forces a moment of actual reading, because the sentence has to be understood before it can be filed away. Since the break is mild and lands back on the subject, following it costs the reader nothing, and the attention it buys carries forward into the next line, which is usually where the real argument sits.
techniques.lands_when: The break is short and returns to the point, so the reader gets the odd note and the message in the same breath.; The off-register line still fits the voice the brand already uses, so it reads as personality rather than as an error.; It arrives where the reader has just settled into a predictable rhythm, often the opening line or a transition.; The unexpected element connects back to the subject,…
techniques.dilutes_when: The detour runs longer than the message it introduces, and the reader remembers the joke but not the offer.; The tone break clashes with the register the brand keeps everywhere else, so the line reads as a stunt.; Every paragraph carries one, and the interruptions become the pattern rather than breaking it.; The odd line has no route back to the subject, leaving the reader to work out why it was…

examples.excerpt: Product copy for a loafer sock, opened with a pair of questions that pretend the socks are not there.
examples.why: 'Socks?' lands as a single word question, then 'What Socks?' cancels the noun it just introduced, and the reader stalls a half beat to resolve a contradiction the copy created about itself. The tell is the size and the source of the break: four words, two fra…

examples.excerpt: A business newsletter item about young adults moving back in with their parents, introduced by a film reference.
examples.why: 'Finally,' opens on a resolution the reader has not been waiting for, and 'a homecoming story that doesn't star Matt Damon' defines the subject by what it excludes, so attention re-seats itself before any actual subject arrives. The tell is scale and register…

techniques.name: The Non-Sequitur
techniques.lede: A line that seems to have nothing to do with what is being sold, so the reader keeps going just to find out why it is there.
techniques.what_it_does: It puts a jarring, apparently unrelated statement or image in front of the reader, with no product, benefit, or context attached to it. Because the line does not connect to an offer the reader can name, it opens a gap. The brain treats an unexplained line as an unfinished thought and stays engaged to close it. The irrelevance is not a flaw to be excused later; it is the whole mechanism. The copy then earns attention by slowly revealing the link the line withheld.
techniques.why_it_works: The mind is built to seek coherence, so a statement that refuses to fit triggers an itch to resolve it. A reader who has already been told a benefit can skim; a reader who cannot yet see why a line is on the page cannot. The gap between what was said and what it could possibly mean becomes a small open loop, and open loops pull the eye forward. Surprise also sharpens memory, so the strange opener tends to stick while a conventional one slides past. The reader keeps reading to relieve the confusion the writer planted on purpose.
techniques.lands_when: The opener sits in the very first position, before any product or context softens it; The line genuinely seems unrelated to the offer, not just colorful or clever; The connection is real and gets paid off, so the reader feels rewarded rather than tricked; The surrounding copy is otherwise clear, so the strangeness reads as deliberate
techniques.dilutes_when: The opener is merely quirky but still plainly on-topic, so no real gap opens; The irrelevance is never resolved and the reader feels jerked around for nothing; Every line is jarring, so the opener loses its contrast and stops interrupting; The strange image is funny on its own and the joke, not the missing link, carries the line

examples.why: The line opens cold with an absurd, unrelated declaration, 'Bigfoot the legendary Sasquatch is real', dropping a claim that connects to nothing the reader expected from marketing copy and forcing attention by sheer disorientation. The structural tell is that…

examples.why: An investing post opens on a writing book, 'Nobody Wants to Read Your Shit', a subject with no visible connection to markets, and lets the mismatch sit until the copy itself asks 'Now, what does any of this have to do with investing?' The reader holds an unfi…

techniques.name: Forced Pause
techniques.lede: A break in the copy that stops the reader for a beat before the next words arrive.
techniques.what_it_does: The writer cuts the line short and leaves a small piece of language standing by itself: a single connecting word, a one word question, or a short fragment placed after the sentence has already closed. Layout does the rest, with a break or extra space where grammar would have carried the reader forward. The stop is the point. The reader has to halt, hold the gap for a beat, and carry the weight of what was just said into whatever comes next.
techniques.why_it_works: Reading runs on momentum, and a long unbroken line invites skimming. A hard stop takes the momentum away, so the reader has to process the last words before moving on. The silence also does work the words do not, because a gap asks the reader to finish the thought, and a conclusion the reader supplies feels more like their own. Short isolated language reads as deliberate, the way a speaker who stops mid sentence is heard as meaning something by the stop itself.
techniques.lands_when: The line before the break has built something worth stopping on, so the silence has weight to hold; The pause sits at a turn, right before a reversal, an admission, or an answer the reader is waiting for; The isolated words are short and plain, so the stop reads as chosen rather than as an accident of formatting; The surrounding copy moves at speed, so the halt registers as a change in pace
techniques.dilutes_when: Every line is clipped the same way, so no single stop stands out from the rest; The break lands mid thought with nothing waiting on the other side, and the reader just feels dropped; The pause is set around a line that carries no weight, which makes the silence look like decoration; The format reflows or closes the gap, so the break the writer set never reaches the reader

examples.headline: Unless we do, we die.
examples.excerpt: An agency statement in print closes one thought as a maxim, then breaks the line before a short warning lands by itself.
examples.why: The line halts the reader by shrinking to five words and ending on 'we die.' The clause opens with a condition, 'Unless we do,' then closes before the reader can carry momentum forward, so the full stop lands as a wall rather than a transition. The structural…

examples.why: The sentence finishes clean at 'the game winning shot', and the full stop hands the reader a complete, flattering picture. Then 'And missed.' arrives as its own sentence, so the reader has to stop, reload, and take the reversal separately. The tell is punctua…

examples.excerpt: A single conjunction stands alone in an online insurance film at the point where the story turns.
examples.why: The copy sets one conjunction alone on the line and closes it with a period. 'But.' is punctuated as a finished sentence even though it finishes nothing, so the eye stops where it expects to keep moving, and the held breath becomes the beat the reader feels.…

techniques.name: Cringe Hook
techniques.lede: A line that makes the reader wince, betting that social discomfort holds attention better than interest does.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy puts in front of the reader something a careful writer would normally cut: a bodily word said plainly, an overshare in a quoted voice, an imagined moment of public humiliation, or a straight-faced performance of a genre people mock. Nothing gets softened and no apology follows. The awkwardness is not a side effect of the message, it is what the message is built on. The reader flinches, and the flinch is what holds them in place long enough for the next line to arrive.
techniques.why_it_works: Embarrassment is involuntary. A reader can skip a claim they doubt and scroll past an offer they do not want, but a line that makes them squirm has already been processed before any decision to keep reading. The discomfort also leaves a small open question: is this person serious, and is it about to get worse. Answering that costs one more line of attention, which is all the opening needs. And because most commercial writing is groomed to be inoffensive, the awkward line sounds like something said rather than something approved.
techniques.lands_when: The awkward thing is stated in specific plain words rather than hinted at or dressed up.; The piece has somewhere to go afterward, so the wince opens onto a point instead of sitting alone.; The audience already accepts blunt or joking talk from this sender, so the line reads as voice and not as a mistake.; The discomfort points at a shared human situation the reader recognizes rather than at the…
techniques.dilutes_when: The writer flags the awkwardness first, with something like 'this may sound a bit odd', which drains it before it arrives.; Every message opens the same way, so the wince becomes house style and stops registering.; The taboo has no connection to what is being sold, leaving a joke with no destination.; The line shames the reader about themselves instead of inviting them into the discomfort.

examples.why: Naming 'my cervix' in a line meant for strangers drags a private clinical body part into public address, and the yardstick 'no larger than my little fingernail' makes the reader measure it against their own hand. The flinch is the point: attention arrives thr…

techniques.name: Warning List
techniques.lede: A counted or bulleted run of danger signs, symptoms, or mistakes, laid out so a reader can scan it and find at least one that fits.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy lists what is going wrong: signs, symptoms, red flags, or errors, sometimes under a stated count and sometimes left open. Each item works as its own small question the reader answers about themselves. Where a count is stated, it promises the set is complete; either way, the spread of items raises the odds that one of them lands. Nothing has to be proved yet. The reader supplies the proof by recognizing an item from their own life, which turns a general claim into a personal diagnosis.
techniques.why_it_works: Recognition is faster than persuasion. A reader who spots one familiar item has already agreed that something is wrong, and they agreed in their own words rather than the writer's. The number does quiet work too: it says someone has counted, sorted, and closed the set, so the list reads as knowledge rather than opinion. Scanning costs almost nothing, so people who would never read a paragraph will read six short lines. Once a single item lands, everything after it is read as being about them.
techniques.lands_when: The items are things a reader can check today in their own body, bank account, or inbox, not abstractions.; The list is wide enough that most of the intended audience hits at least one, and narrow enough that hitting one actually means something.; The count is stated and the list delivers exactly that many, so the promise of completeness holds up.; Each item is short and concrete, so the whole se…
techniques.dilutes_when: The items are vague states like stress or feeling stuck that fit everyone, so recognition carries no information.; The list is a benefit stack in disguise, praising the product instead of naming what is wrong.; The count is inflated and the later items repeat the earlier ones, which tells the reader the set was padded to reach the number.; The reader is handed a symptom with no next step, so the…

techniques.name: Provocative Statistics
techniques.lede: A single data point, chosen and framed so it collides with what the reader took for granted, forcing a quick rewrite of their picture of how things really are.
techniques.what_it_does: It states a number the reader did not see coming: a share, a count, or a rate that contradicts a settled belief about how common, how large, or how broken something is. The figure is not offered as proof of a claim, it is the claim itself, a small fact that makes the familiar suddenly strange. The reader stops to square the number with what they thought they knew, and that pause is the gap the rest of the message walks through.
techniques.why_it_works: Surprise is what makes a fact stick. A number that fits our expectations passes straight through us, while a number that breaks them opens a gap between belief and reality that the mind wants to close. That itch buys attention and a moment of doubt about assumptions the reader never examined. Because it is a figure and not an opinion, it feels checkable and neutral, so it slips past the guard people raise against a pitch. Having conceded the surprising fact, the reader is readier to accept whatever argument is built on top of it.
techniques.lands_when: The number genuinely contradicts a widely held assumption, rather than just stating a big or frightening figure.; The statistic sits up front and the rest of the copy is built to resolve or exploit the surprise it creates.; The figure is specific and sourced enough to read as real rather than invented for effect.; The gap between what the reader expected and what the number says is wide and easy…
techniques.dilutes_when: The figure only confirms what the reader already believed, so there is no jolt.; The number is there to prove a product claim instead of overturning a belief, which makes it ordinary proof.; So many statistics are stacked that no single one lands as a reordering shock.; The stat is vague, rounded, or unsourced enough that the reader discounts it rather than feeling surprised.

techniques.name: Competitor Composition Attack
techniques.lede: Attack a rival by naming, and often measuring, the cheap filler inside its product, so the buyer suddenly sees what they have really been paying for.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy takes a rival product apart and names its worthless part: the water, the sugar, the bun, the dead padding, the underdosed active ingredient. Often it puts a number on that part; sometimes it just itemizes or names the filler plainly and lets the list speak for itself. Either way it sets its own composition against the rival's. A buyer who never thought to ask suddenly sees that much of what they paid for was filler. The concrete detail carries the accusation, and the counter-claim about the seller's own product collects the trust the accusation just freed up.
techniques.why_it_works: Quantification turns a vague suspicion into a fact the buyer cannot unsee. A percentage or a fraction feels checkable and fair, so the attack reads as information rather than a smear, and the reader lowers the guard they would raise against plain bragging. It also reframes the past: every earlier purchase becomes a small overpayment, which stings more than any claim of being better. And it hands the buyer a durable test they can carry back to the shelf, so the seller wins not one comparison but every future one.
techniques.lands_when: The filler figure is specific and checkable, not a round guess.; The named component is something the buyer did not realize they were paying for.; A clean counter-claim about the seller's own composition follows the attack.; The category genuinely hides cheap padding behind a premium price.
techniques.dilutes_when: The percentage is vague or obviously invented, so it reads as a smear.; The seller's own product cannot survive the same teardown.; The filler named is one buyers already expect and accept.; The attack sprawls into general trash-talk instead of one measured component.

techniques.name: The Off-Topic Hook
techniques.lede: A passage about something with no visible connection to the offer, held open until the copy reveals the link.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy goes somewhere the reader did not expect: a personal memory, a forwarded article, a short parable, a passage from a book, or an odd thing that happened to a stranger. None of it names the product or the problem it solves. Some versions say out loud that the story led somewhere, so the reader knows a connection is coming. Others simply begin telling it and leave the relevance unstated. Either way the reader carries an unanswered question forward: why am I being told this?
techniques.why_it_works: A reader who expects a pitch has defenses ready for a pitch. An ordinary story does not trip them, so it gets read on its own terms. The missing connection then does the work, because people tend to finish a pattern once it is started, and an opening with no visible relevance is an unfinished pattern. Reading on is the only way to close it. By the time the link appears, the reader has already spent attention on the story, so the offer arrives inside something they chose to follow rather than something pushed at them.
techniques.lands_when: The opening subject is specific and concrete, so it holds attention on its own while the connection is still hidden.; The link, when it arrives, is real and worth the wait, so the detour reads as a point rather than a stall.; The story is short enough that the unanswered question stays interesting instead of turning into impatience.; The reader already trusts the sender enough to grant a few sent…
techniques.dilutes_when: The tangent has no honest connection and the bridge is forced, which reads as a trick and costs trust.; The opening runs long, so the reader gives up before the payoff arrives.; The same audience has seen the move so often that an unrelated start now announces that a pitch is coming.; The story is generic and interchangeable, so there is nothing to hold the reader while the relevance is withheld.

techniques.name: Category Reversal Premise
techniques.lede: The copy names the way its category has always worked, then presents the brand as the deliberate opposite of that way.
techniques.what_it_does: The move has two beats delivered in one breath. First it names a specific norm, the standard practice the whole category follows: the pricing habit, the supply chain, the tone, the rule everybody obeys. Then it points at the brand as that norm's inversion: we do the reverse. The reader is handed a small map of the market with every rival grouped on one side and this brand alone on the other, defined by the practice it refuses.
techniques.why_it_works: A named norm gives the reader something concrete to check against their own experience, so the claim of difference feels observed rather than asserted. Contrast then does the positioning work: once the category is framed as one undifferentiated mass, the brand owns the only slot left, the opposite pole. The frame also recruits the reader; agreeing that the old way is broken makes choosing the brand feel like taking a side rather than buying a product. And because the stated difference is structural, not cosmetic, it reads as a reason the offer must be better.
techniques.lands_when: The named norm is real and the reader recognizes it from their own experience of the category.; The brand genuinely operates differently, so the reversal claim survives a quick check.; The category is crowded with lookalikes, which makes a single clear opposite stand out.; The norm is specific: a pricing habit, a process step, a design rule, not a vague mood.
techniques.dilutes_when: The norm is invented or too vague to verify, so the setup reads as a straw man.; Every rival in the category also claims to be the exception, and the reversal becomes wallpaper.; The copy names the norm but never says what the brand does instead, leaving the contrast half built.; The actual product experience matches the very norm the copy claims to reject.

techniques.name: The Tangent Bridge
techniques.lede: The Tangent Bridge starts the copy somewhere the reader did not expect, then swings that far-off subject back to the offer with a link that feels obvious the moment it lands.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy opens inside a subject that has nothing to do with what is being sold: a war, a bad joke, an ancient religious order, a famous man in another industry. It stays there long enough for the reader to settle in. Then a hinge line ties the outside subject to the reader's own situation, and the offer arrives already carrying the meaning of the tangent. Two things travel across the bridge at once: attention, and a new way of naming what the offer is.
techniques.why_it_works: A reader who has decided this is an ad stops reading ads. A story about something else is not an ad yet, so the guard stays down. The gap between the two subjects also creates a small question the reader wants answered: what does this have to do with me. Holding that question keeps them in the copy until the hinge pays it off. And because the reader takes the last step of the connection themselves, the conclusion feels like their own thought rather than a claim they were handed.
techniques.lands_when: The opening subject is genuinely far from the offer, so the pivot is a surprise rather than a restatement; One clear hinge line names the connection out loud instead of leaving the reader to guess; The connection survives inspection: the two things really do share the same underlying shape; The tangent changes how the offer is understood, not just how the page begins
techniques.dilutes_when: The copy wanders off topic and never builds the bridge back, leaving a story with no point; The tangent is only decoration and the offer would read the same with it cut; The link is forced, so the reader spends their attention arguing with the comparison instead of accepting it; The detour runs so long that the reader leaves before the payoff arrives

techniques.name: The Re-Engagement Question
techniques.lede: A question dropped into the middle of running copy and aimed straight at the reader, to pull drifting attention back.
techniques.what_it_does: Long copy turns the reader into a spectator. A direct question turns them back into a participant. The writer stops narrating and asks something the reader has to answer in their own head: what they want, what they just thought, what they would do next. The question is usually short, second person, and set apart from the sentences around it. It does not need an answer on the page. Its job is to reset attention at the exact point where interest was about to slide.
techniques.why_it_works: A question opens a loop the mind closes on its own. Reading is passive, being asked something is not. The moment the question lands, the reader supplies an answer before deciding whether to, and that answer belongs to them, so whatever the copy says next arrives as agreement rather than as a claim. Direct address also breaks the rhythm of the page, and a broken rhythm gets noticed. Placement carries more weight than wording: the question buys back attention precisely where a long passage was losing it.
techniques.lands_when: It falls where attention naturally dips, after a long stretch of proof, story, or detail.; It asks something the reader can answer instantly out of their own life, with no thinking required.; The wording is short and second person, so it reads as a turn toward the reader rather than one more line of pitch.; The copy that follows treats the reader's silent answer as settled and builds on it.

techniques.name: Era-Shift Obsolescence Frame
techniques.lede: Name a past era and pronounce its playbook dead, so today's reader feels the old way slipping out from under them.
techniques.what_it_does: This move points at a specific past time, a named year, decade, or labeled era, and declares its methods finished. It does not merely promise something new. It retires the old explicitly, drawing a line between a then that no longer works and a now that does. The reader's current frustration gets reframed as a symptom of running on yesterday's tools rather than any failing of their own, which makes switching feel less like a choice and more like catching up to a change that already happened.
techniques.why_it_works: People hate being left behind more than they fear trying something unproven. By dating the old way and calling it over, the copy converts a hard sell into a simple update: you are not wrong, you are just out of date. That framing sidesteps defensiveness, because the enemy is a moment in time rather than the reader. It also borrows the authority of inevitability. If an era has genuinely ended, resisting looks foolish, and the new option inherits the momentum of history moving in one direction.
techniques.lands_when: A specific year, decade, or named era anchors the claim, so the obsolescence feels factual rather than vague.; The reader's stalled results are recast as a symptom of old tools, not personal failure.; The market actually turns over fast (ads, search, software), so the dead-playbook claim is credible.; The new way is named as the thing the new era runs on, giving the reader somewhere to step.
techniques.dilutes_when: The copy promises newness but never names what era it is replacing, collapsing into generic hype.; The declared shift is not believable, so the reader reads bluster instead of a real turn.; It only scolds the reader for being late without retiring any actual past method.; Nostalgia creeps in and the old era sounds better than the new one being sold.

techniques.name: Domestic Scene Drop-In
techniques.lede: The copy lands inside a household moment already in progress, letting the scene carry the ad instead of a narrator.
techniques.what_it_does: The words land inside a household moment that is already running. Sometimes a person speaks and the reader arrives mid-sentence; sometimes the room itself gets shown, with its noise and its hour. Nothing sets the scene up. The reader fills in the kitchen, the couple, the children from a handful of words, and the ordinary friction or oddity of the moment holds attention long enough for the seller to arrive, whether that comes in the next breath or much later.
techniques.why_it_works: A reader braced for a pitch drops the guard when the opening is not one. Household moments come pre-furnished: most people have run short of something at the wrong hour, or heard that tone of voice across a room, so the copy borrows a whole setting at the cost of a line. Overhearing also flatters. The reader becomes a witness rather than a target, and a witness leans in to work out who is talking and what just happened. Attention gets spent on the scene, not on resisting the sale.

techniques.name: Prior Approach Invalidation
techniques.lede: A short qualifier that splits a familiar category into a right kind and a wrong kind, leaving the reader to suspect that the version they already own is the wrong one.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy takes something the reader already uses or already treats as settled, then draws a line inside it. A variety, a component, a fit, a habit, or a standard remedy gets sorted, and the reader's own version lands on the losing side. The shapes vary: one right variety among many, an overlooked input quietly spoiling the result, a size most people get wrong, or an accepted answer the copy steps past. Acting without the correct specification starts to look pointless.
techniques.why_it_works: It works on prior investment rather than on ignorance. The reader has already bought the thing, adopted the habit, or closed the question, so the copy never has to argue for the category. It concedes the category and moves the argument down one level, to the version. That is a smaller claim and an easier one to accept, and accepting it opens a gap the reader cannot close alone, because the correct specification sits with the seller. Sometimes the wrong version is named outright, often it is only implied.
techniques.lands_when: The reader already owns the thing or already does it, so the copy can concede the category and argue only about the version.; The line it draws is checkable: a variety, a size, a component, a grade, rather than a vague claim of being better.; The wrong version is one the reader plausibly has, so the doubt attaches to something specific in their own life.; The correct specification is something th…
techniques.dilutes_when: The reader has no prior version to invalidate, so the qualifier catches nothing.; The distinction is asserted with no detail about what separates the right kind from the wrong kind.; It reads as an attack on the reader's judgment instead of on the version they were sold.; Every seller in the category runs the same line, so saying not all of these are the same stops carrying information.

techniques.name: Symptom Escalation Hook
techniques.lede: A small, familiar symptom the reader already has gets named, then reframed as the early sign of a far bigger problem.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy names a minor complaint the reader recognizes in themselves, a habit, an ache, a passing sign, and then reveals it as a warning of something serious. It casts the net wide, often asking whether you have ever felt the thing, so almost everyone qualifies, and it raises the stakes in the same breath. The trivial detail becomes evidence of a hidden condition. That turns an ordinary reader into an at-risk one who now has a personal reason to keep reading.
techniques.why_it_works: Two forces fire at once. The small symptom works as a mirror: the reader sees themselves in it, so the message feels personally true rather than generic. Then the jump to something serious loads that recognition with fear, and the gap between how minor it felt and how grave it might be creates a need to resolve the uncertainty. Because the qualifying language stays broad, the audience widens while each person feels singled out. The reader continues not to learn about a product but to find out whether they are in danger.
techniques.lands_when: The named symptom is genuinely common and easy to recognize in oneself; The jump from minor to serious stays plausible enough to believe, not cartoonish; The stakes named are ones the reader already fears, such as aging, disease, or decline; The escalation arrives fast, in the first line, before doubt has time to set in
techniques.dilutes_when: The opening symptom is rare or vague, so few readers see themselves in it; The serious claim overreaches and reads as a scare, which breaks trust; The link between the symptom and the danger is asserted but never made believable; The wording qualifies so narrowly, such as constantly or severe, that it shrinks the audience it needs

techniques.name: Setup-Then-Overlooked Pivot
techniques.lede: Grant a familiar topic its due, then turn the reader toward the neighbor it has been overshadowing.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy names something the audience already respects or hears about constantly, states it plainly, and does not argue with it. Then it swings attention to a related item that gets far less notice and hands that one the emphasis. The turn takes several shapes: a plain contrast between what everyone discusses and what nobody does, a pair of halves where the second is said to count as much, a list whose final item is flagged as the overlooked one, or an accepted rule carried over to a second subject.
techniques.why_it_works: The opening claim is one the reader already holds, so agreement is instant and costs nothing. The pivot then travels on that agreement instead of starting a fresh argument: the second item arrives inside a frame the reader has just accepted, which is easier than earning attention cold. Naming the overlooked item outright gives the reader a word for something vague they may have half noticed, and that reads as a discovery rather than a pitch. Because the setup is left standing, nothing invites the reader to argue back.
techniques.lands_when: The setup names something the audience genuinely respects or has heard plenty about, so agreeing with it costs nothing; The overlooked item sits close enough to the setup that the standing of the first carries over to the second; The pivot names the second thing outright rather than pointing at a blank and asking the reader to wonder; The second half gets the weight: it lands last, and the copy g…
techniques.dilutes_when: The setup is built only to be knocked down, which turns the move into an argument the reader can resist; The overlooked item is the setup under a new label, so the reader hears one idea said twice; The turn arrives with nothing named, leaving a tease where the payoff belongs; The respected topic runs so long that it becomes the subject of the piece and the pivot reads as an afterthought

techniques.name: The Big Claim
techniques.lede: State an outcome so large that the reader keeps reading just to find out whether it could possibly be true.
techniques.what_it_does: Big Claim states a result pushed to its outer edge: a number, a multiple, or an end-state stated at full size and offered without apology. Instead of easing the reader toward belief, it plants a flag the reader cannot ignore, betting that an outcome this bold is more arresting than a modest one is credible. The size of the promise becomes the hook. Disbelief itself turns into attention, because the reader has to keep going to settle whether the claim holds up.
techniques.why_it_works: A claim at full magnitude creates an open question the mind wants closed. The reader's skepticism, the very reaction that should end interest, instead keeps them in the copy, hunting for the catch or the proof. A bold figure also sets the anchor: even if the reader discounts it, the discounted version still feels large. And a falsifiable outcome reads as confidence, since a writer who names an exact result appears to have something real behind it. The promise has to be specific enough to picture and audacious enough to doubt.
techniques.lands_when: The outcome is concrete and falsifiable, a figure or end-state the reader can picture and mentally audit; The magnitude is pushed to the edge of belief, large enough that disbelief becomes curiosity; Proof, mechanism, or a track record stands ready to catch the reader who keeps reading to test the claim; The promise targets a result the reader already wants badly, so the size feels like hope rath…
techniques.dilutes_when: The outcome is abstract or metaphorical, with no size the reader can check; It collapses into a bare superlative or exclusivity claim that names a posture, not a result; The figure is hedged with 'up to' or 'as much as' until the bold number carries no weight; No proof or reason follows, so the claim reads as empty bluster and the reader disengages

techniques.name: Reply or Forward Frame
techniques.lede: A first approach dressed as a reply, so the message lands looking like a conversation the reader is already part of.
techniques.what_it_does: The line borrows the inbox's own grammar for continued mail. Often that is a literal Re: or RE: sitting in front of a short fragment. Sometimes it is a status word that belongs to transactional mail, or a question that treats an earlier step as already taken. Either way the line points back at something as though the reader knows what it is, and the thing pointed at goes unnamed or barely named. The pitch is withheld. What arrives has the shape of correspondence rather than the shape of an ad.
techniques.why_it_works: Inbox scanning sorts mail into owed and optional before anything is really read, and a reply belongs to the owed pile, because a thread implies the reader started it. The frame also plants a small gap, since the subject points at something the reader cannot identify from the line alone, and opening is the cheapest way to settle it. Presupposition does the rest. A line that assumes the earlier exchange is harder to wave off at a glance than a line that asks for one, because refusing it means first deciding it is false.
techniques.lands_when: Some plausible prior contact exists, a list the reader joined or a form they filled, so the claim of a thread is not absurd on its face.; The thing referred back to is short and specific enough that the reader tries to place it and cannot.; The body keeps the voice the subject promised instead of switching to broadcast sales copy on the first line.; The sender reaches for the frame rarely, so the…
techniques.dilutes_when: No earlier exchange exists and the body cannot support the claim, so the open is followed by the feeling of being tricked.; Every send from the same address wears the same prefix, and the signal stops registering as anything but a house tic.; The subject misleads about what the message actually contains, which is the thing email law and mailbox providers police most directly.; The line promises a…

techniques.name: Threaded-Voicemail Reply
techniques.lede: Threaded-Voicemail Reply frames a cold message as though it were the next turn in a conversation the reader already started.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy borrows the shape of a reply, a personal response, or a check-in, so the inbox reads it as a continuation rather than a pitch. It plants a small 'you already know what this is about' cue: a subject line answering a message never sent, a personal reply that names the recipient, or a check-in that presumes a conversation already underway. The reader fills in the missing prior turn, and that invented history makes the message feel owed a response.
techniques.why_it_works: People treat an open loop as a small debt. A message that appears to arrive mid-thread triggers the reflex to catch up and reply, because ignoring a reply feels ruder than ignoring an ad. The faked continuity slips past the cold-open filter, since the reader's guard is set for strangers selling, not for someone resuming a talk. Naming a person or a past event borrows the trust of a relationship that was never formed. Curiosity finishes the job, because the reader must open the message to rebuild the thread they cannot remember.
techniques.lands_when: The cue names a specific prior turn the reader could plausibly have had: a call, a reply, a mailing from a set date.; The channel matches the fiction, so a supposed reply arrives where real replies live.; The invented history is small and ordinary enough to feel forgotten rather than fabricated.; Opening the message is the only way to resolve who or what the thread refers to.
techniques.dilutes_when: The reply prefix sits on a subject line that plainly began no conversation, so it reads as a gimmick.; The claimed prior contact is grand or implausible, breaking the sense of a resumed private channel.; The body abandons the thread fiction at once and becomes a standard pitch.; Warm tone or first-name address stands in for real faked continuity, leaving familiarity with no thread to resume.

techniques.name: Editorial Format Borrowed Trust
techniques.lede: Dress the ad in the clothes of a news article so the reader trusts it before they know it is selling something.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy borrows the look and shape of journalism. It uses a city and state dateline, a reporter-style byline, an article headline with a sub-deck, a third-person news sentence that front-loads the facts, or a quotation credited to a named publication. None of it is a column the reader chose to read, yet it arrives wearing the format the reader associates with reported fact. By the time the piece reveals it is an advertisement, the trust heuristics tuned for editorial pages have already engaged and softened the usual sales resistance.
techniques.why_it_works: Readers run different filters for news and for ads. A reported article triggers a posture of learning, while an ad triggers a posture of defense. Format is the cue that flips the switch, and people read format faster than they read intent, so the journalistic shell does its work before the skeptical filter wakes up. The borrowed authority of a dateline or a credited quote also transfers, so a claim that would sound like a boast in ad voice reads as a finding in news voice. The reader lowers their guard for the structure, not the seller.
techniques.lands_when: The news label sits on copy that actually reports something, a finding, an event, a named source, so the borrowed format has content to carry.; The category is one where fresh information genuinely changes a decision, such as health, money, or supply.; The styling fits the channel it appears in, a printed page that reads like a page, an inbox line that reads like a bulletin.; The reader is cold a…
techniques.dilutes_when: The label is pasted onto an ordinary offer with no event behind it, and the reader feels the swap in the next sentence.; The audience already treats every message from this sender as promotion, so the news costume has no cover left.; The stamp and the story disagree, for example a fresh date attached to an item the reader saw months ago.; The setting requires the ad to be marked as an ad, so the…

techniques.name: Behavioral-Departure Curiosity Hook
techniques.lede: The copy points to a break from the obvious choice, often made by a named person or group, then refuses to say what replaced it.
techniques.what_it_does: Two things have to be present: an ordinary default the copy reports as abandoned, and a replacement that stays unnamed. Often the party doing the abandoning is a specific person or group the reader would like to be counted among; sometimes the copy simply tells the reader the default no longer applies to them. Either way, the reader learns that a switch has already happened and is not told what the switch was. The sentence ends on the withheld half, so the only way to close it is to keep reading. The departure is the news; the alternative is the bait.
techniques.why_it_works: Two pressures stack in one line. The missing half opens a question the reader did not ask and now cannot easily drop, which is harder to ignore than a plain claim. The people doing the leaving are chosen so the reader wants to be one of them, so the gap becomes a status problem: they already know, you do not. The unnamed replacement collects credit it has not yet earned, because a reader filling in a blank fills it with something better than what they currently have.
techniques.lands_when: The group named is specific enough to picture and one the reader already wants to belong to.; The thing being left behind is a genuine default, the choice most readers assume is simply what you do.; The replacement is held back completely, with no adjective that lets the reader guess it.; The answer arrives quickly, on the next line or the next screen, and really does name the alternative.
techniques.dilutes_when: The alternative is named in the same breath, which closes the gap before it can pull.; The abandoned option is not a default anyone actually holds, so leaving it signals nothing.; The group is vague, like people or smart shoppers, so there is no inside to be outside of.; The shape repeats in every subject line until readers learn the withheld thing is rarely worth the click.

techniques.name: Hard Pattern Interrupt
techniques.lede: States the line its setting forbids, saying the opposite of what the reader has been trained to expect there, so the message cannot be processed on autopilot.
techniques.what_it_does: Every setting carries a script. A car advertisement praises the car. A health mailing reassures. A nutrition ad sympathizes with the busy parent. This technique writes the line the script rules out and states it flatly. The contradiction is not decoration laid over a compliant line, it replaces the compliant line. The reader arrives holding a prediction about what the message will say, and the words refute it. Reading has to slow down before the message can be filed or waved away.
techniques.why_it_works: People read familiar formats by prediction rather than by attention. The mind guesses the next few words from the format, confirms the guess with a glance, and moves on. That is how a whole page of advertising gets skipped without ever being read. A direct contradiction breaks the guess. The prediction fails, the automatic pass stops, and the words have to be handled consciously while the reader works out what is going on. The pull is not the shock itself, it is the gap the shock opens, which the reader now wants closed.
techniques.lands_when: The line contradicts something the setting itself promised, not just something odd in general.; The message can honestly justify the contradiction within the next few lines.; The contradiction points straight at the real argument, so the jolt and the sale are the same thing.; The audience knows the format well enough to hold a prediction worth breaking.
techniques.dilutes_when: The opening is merely loud or strange rather than a contradiction of anything specific.; The contradiction has nothing to do with what follows, so the reader feels played and leaves.; One brand runs the move so often that the interruption becomes the expected pattern.; It is a bare insult or shock with no argument behind it to earn the attention it takes.
