techniques.name: Handbook as Primary Marketing Surface
techniques.lede: The company hands outsiders the document it wrote for its own staff, and that internal manual does the selling.
techniques.what_it_does: The brand takes a document it wrote for its own people, the operations manual, the rules of the house, the way work actually gets done, and hands it to outsiders as the pitch. The copy points at that document, names it plainly, and often gives one fact about it: how long it is, why it exists, or how much it matters inside the company. Shapes vary. It can be the full manual, a short public note that the manual exists, or a printed sheet of working rules.
techniques.why_it_works: A manual written for people who have to use it reads differently from a brochure. It is long, specific, and dull in places, and a reader takes that as a sign it was not staged for them. Handing it over also puts a stranger inside the company before any purchase, which moves the question from whether the claims are true to whether this way of working suits them. When the copy also invites corrections, the document reads as something kept in the open rather than approved for release.
techniques.lands_when: The document already exists for internal use and would read the same whether or not a prospect ever saw it; How the company works is itself part of what is being bought, so the manual is the product demonstration; The copy names the document and tells the reader they can go read it, instead of describing its openness in the abstract; Something in it can be checked, such as its length, the reason…
techniques.dilutes_when: The document is written for prospects first, so it reads as a brochure with chapter headings; The copy claims openness but the pages behind the link are thin, generic, or long out of date; The material describes how the company would like to work rather than how it does; Everyone in the category publishes one, so having a handbook stops being a signal and becomes the price of entry

techniques.name: Identity Badge
techniques.lede: Frame owning or wearing the product as a visible badge that announces which group the buyer belongs to.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy turns the product into a membership marker. Instead of selling what the thing does, it sells what owning it says about you to other people. It names a group worth joining, a patriot, an elite, a member, a tribe, and ties the product to that label so that buying it reads as claiming the identity. The object becomes a signal others can see and recognize. The pitch is less about function and more about who you get to be, and who will know it.
techniques.why_it_works: People buy things to tell others, and themselves, who they are. A badge gives the purchase a social payoff that outlasts the product itself: every time it is seen, it repeats the claim. Naming the group does two jobs at once. It flatters the buyer with a flattering label, and it promises recognition from the people who already wear the badge. The move borrows the pull of belonging, the wish to be counted among a desirable few, and attaches it to an item you can hold, wear, or show. Identity is stickier than any feature.
techniques.lands_when: The product is something worn, carried, or shown where others can read the signal; A specific, desirable group is named or clearly evoked, not just a vague good feeling; The buyer already wants to be seen as that kind of person; The badge promises recognition from insiders who share the identity
techniques.dilutes_when: The group is so broad that belonging to it signals nothing; The copy leans on crowd-size counts, so it reads as social proof rather than identity; The reward is a discount or perk, making access the point instead of belonging; The claimed identity clashes with what the product actually is or costs

techniques.name: Grow-With-You Relationship Promise
techniques.lede: A promise that the product will change and keep up as the buyer's life or business changes, so one purchase becomes a companion for years rather than a transaction.
techniques.what_it_does: This move repositions the purchase from a one-time exchange to a long relationship. The copy claims the product has stages, headroom, or learning built in, so its value keeps pace as the buyer's situation shifts: a child gets older, a company scales, a life stage turns over. The structural signature is a stated span or arc, such as an age range, a start-to-maturity journey, or a pledge to stay alongside the buyer, that makes future fit part of what is being bought today.
techniques.why_it_works: Buyers hesitate because they can picture outgrowing the thing in front of them, and replacing it later feels like paying twice. This promise answers that fear before it is voiced: you will not have to switch, re-learn, or re-buy. It also recruits the buyer's future self as a reason to act now, since the purchase is framed as serving years of coming needs, not just today's. And once a product is felt as a companion on a journey, leaving it registers as a loss, which quietly raises loyalty and lifetime value.
techniques.lands_when: The buyer's situation predictably changes over years, such as a growing child, a scaling company, or a shifting life stage, and the product genuinely has modes or headroom to match.; Switching later would be costly or disruptive, so a credible "you will never outgrow us" answers a fear the buyer already carries.; The claim is anchored in concrete spans, stages, or mechanisms (an age range, a conv…
techniques.dilutes_when: The product is short-lived or single-use, so a years-long promise reads as inflated and undermines trust in the rest of the copy.; Every competitor makes the same "scales with you" claim in the same words, turning the promise into category wallpaper with no differentiating force.; No mechanism for adaptation is shown, so the reader has no way to believe the product will actually change alongside…

techniques.name: Catchphrase Product Pun
techniques.lede: A famous line the reader can already finish gets bent so its punchline lands on the product's name, category, or offer.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy borrows a phrase the audience already knows by heart: a song lyric, a show title, a slogan, a saying from somewhere else entirely. Then it swaps one word or one sound so the line now points at the product, its name, or the action the ad wants taken. The borrowed phrase does the attention work, because recognition is instant, and the swap does the selling work, because the twist puts the brand exactly where the familiar ending used to sit.
techniques.why_it_works: Familiar phrases are processed with almost no effort, and easy processing feels good, so the reader gets a small reward just for recognizing the line. The twist adds a second reward: the reader completes the joke in their own head, which makes the brand feel clever by association and makes the line easy to repeat to someone else. Because the punchline sits on the product itself, the memory of the joke and the memory of the brand get stored together. The reader cannot recall the gag without recalling what was being sold.
techniques.lands_when: The borrowed phrase is so widely known that the audience finishes it in their head before the swap arrives.; The product name or category genuinely fits the phrase, so the pun feels found rather than forced.; The tone of the source phrase matches the brand's voice and the moment, playful source for a playful pitch.; The line is short enough to survive as a headline, a subject line, or a spoken ta…
techniques.dilutes_when: The reference is niche or dated, so a large share of the audience never hears the original underneath the twist.; The punchline lands on a discount or a benefit instead of the product, so the joke gets remembered and the brand does not.; The stretch is too far and the reader has to work to see the connection, turning a small reward into a chore.; Many brands in the category lean on the same borro…

techniques.name: Internal Monologue Capture
techniques.lede: Internal Monologue Capture writes the sentence the reader is already saying inside their own head, not the tidied version they would say out loud.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy stops describing the reader from the outside and starts speaking in the reader's own head-voice. Instead of naming a problem in seller's language, it writes the exact sentence the reader thinks when the problem shows up: the half-finished question, the private verdict, the small confession nobody hears. Often the writing sets a scene, shows what an onlooker would see, then cuts to the line running underneath it. Recognition of the wording arrives before any judgment of the claim.
techniques.why_it_works: People trust their own thoughts more than anyone else's account of them. When copy repeats a sentence the reader has actually said to themselves, recognition lands before evaluation, and the writer borrows the credibility of the reader's own voice. It also proves knowledge, because only someone who has stood where the reader stands would know the private wording. And since the thought already belongs to the reader, agreeing costs nothing. The reader is not talked into a new idea, they are shown that someone finally said the old one aloud.
techniques.lands_when: The line uses words the reader would actually use, not language cleaned up into brand voice.; The thought is specific enough that only this reader would think it, an exact small moment rather than a general worry.; The copy shows the gap between what an onlooker sees and what the reader is saying underneath.; The wording is lifted from real customer language in reviews, calls, or replies, rather…
techniques.dilutes_when: The quoted thought is a polished slogan nobody has ever thought in that shape.; The copy names the feeling from outside instead of writing the sentence itself.; The guess misses, the reader silently corrects it, and that costs more trust than saying nothing would have.; Quoted thoughts pile up until the reader stops seeing themselves and starts reading a checklist.

techniques.name: Nonnegotiable Belief Assertion
techniques.lede: A belief is stated flat out as settled fact, with the negotiable reading closed off, so the reader can only line up behind it or walk away.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy puts a value on the table as fact rather than opinion, then leaves no room to treat it as debatable. The shapes vary: a flat one-line declarative with nothing after it, an explicit negation of optionality ("not optional", "not a suggestion"), a hard binary that makes the reader choose a side, or an absolute claim with the alternative written off. The point is not argued in any of these. The reader is not invited to weigh the claim, only to sort themselves for or against it.
techniques.why_it_works: Stating a belief as fact skips the argument. There is no evidence on offer to pick apart, only a position to accept or refuse, and refusing means leaving. Readers who already hold the belief feel named and gathered, which is worth more to the writer than the readers who leave. The unhedged wording also signals that the writer will not soften under pressure, and conviction reads as credible even when nothing is proved. Where the copy spells out what happens to people who disagree, the cost of dissent becomes visible and fence-sitters pick a side.
techniques.lands_when: The belief is one a real slice of the audience already holds strongly, so stating it gathers people instead of lecturing them.; The wording closes off the negotiable reading, with phrasing like "not optional", "not a suggestion", or a straight either/or.; The business can afford to lose everyone who disagrees, and would rather have the smaller, aligned audience.; The line stays short and unhedged…
techniques.dilutes_when: The stated belief is bland enough that nobody would disagree, so no one gets sorted and nothing is gained.; Softeners creep in, and "we believe" or "in most cases" turns the fact back into an opinion.; Everything in the copy is pitched as nonnegotiable, so the one belief that mattered is buried in the noise.; The declared value is not matched by how the business behaves, so the line reads as a sl…

techniques.name: Jobs-to-Be-Done Frame
techniques.lede: Identify the reader by the job they are trying to get done, not by who they are.
techniques.what_it_does: This move defines the audience through the task in front of them rather than a demographic or a personality profile. Instead of naming an age, a title, or a set of traits, it names the functional, emotional, or social outcome the reader is trying to reach, and casts the product as the thing hired to reach it. The reader recognizes themselves not by a label but by a goal they already hold, so the copy speaks to a situation and an intention the reader is living inside at the moment of the decision.
techniques.why_it_works: People do not shop for a category; they reach for whatever gets a specific job done. Naming that job makes the reader feel seen at the exact point of intent, which beats any flattering label because it matches the reason they started looking. It sidesteps the identity defenses a demographic pitch triggers, since no one argues with their own goal. It also pre-frames the product as a means to an end the reader already owns, so the purchase reads as hiring help for a task rather than being sold a thing.
techniques.lands_when: The task named is specific and real, one the reader is actively trying to finish right now; It captures the emotional or social stakes of the job, not only the mechanical outcome; The product is positioned as hired help for that job, so the fit is obvious; The situation is drawn tightly enough that the right reader thinks that is exactly me
techniques.dilutes_when: The job is so broad it fits everyone, so it identifies no one in particular; It slides back into a demographic or title label instead of an actual task; It lists product features and forgets to name the outcome the reader wants; It stacks so many jobs at once that no single intent feels addressed

techniques.name: Deep-Belief Confirmation
techniques.lede: The copy tells readers that something they already believe is true, stating it as settled fact instead of arguing for it.
techniques.what_it_does: It takes a conviction the audience already carries, about how the world works or who they are, and says it out loud as though it were obvious. The shape varies. Sometimes the belief is confirmed flat, in a single line. Sometimes it arrives as shared insider knowledge, a we-both-know-this aside. Sometimes the copy names the stance the reader holds toward the brand, then turns it. What the versions share is that the belief is asserted, not proven, and the reader is positioned as having been right all along.
techniques.why_it_works: The feeling is already there. The writer does not have to build conviction from nothing, only point at what the reader is carrying and agree with it. Agreement costs the reader nothing, because saying yes here means saying yes to something they already thought. It also does identity work: whoever says this out loud appears to see the world the way the reader does, which buys attention before any claim about a product is made. Because no argument is offered, there is nothing yet to argue back against.
techniques.lands_when: The belief named is one the audience holds with real feeling, not a mild preference or a fact they would shrug at; The wording sounds like the reader's own private thought rather than a marketer's summary of it; It comes early, before any pitch, so the reader agrees with the writer before being asked for anything; The belief is specific enough that people outside the group would not nod along to…
techniques.dilutes_when: The stated belief is so broad that everyone agrees, so agreeing signals nothing and costs the reader no commitment; The copy starts explaining or defending the belief, which turns a shared truth back into a debate; It flatters a belief the audience does not actually hold, and the reader hears a stranger guessing at them; The validation never connects to what is being sold, leaving a warm opening…

techniques.name: Pre-Qualified "Because" Framing
techniques.lede: The offer names who the reader already is, so accepting feels like continuing a relationship rather than answering a pitch.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy leads with an identity the reader already holds and values, member, subscriber, veteran, longtime customer, cardholder, and treats that identity as the reason the offer exists for them. A word like 'because,' or a stand-in such as 'as a' or 'for,' ties the offer directly to that status. The reader is cast as selected or eligible before any selling starts, so a cold approach becomes a warm continuation of a relationship the reader already recognizes and trusts.
techniques.why_it_works: Because the reader already owns the named identity, going along with the offer simply keeps them consistent with who they are. Being told they are pre-selected flatters and lowers the guard, since people rarely audit a deal that looks already decided in their favor. The frame borrows warmth from a relationship the reader values and recasts a sales approach as a courtesy owed to a member. It also skips the qualifying step: the reader feels already past the gate, so the only remaining question is whether to accept.
techniques.lands_when: The named identity is one the reader genuinely holds and takes some pride in.; The 'because' links that specific identity to the specific offer, not a generic flattery.; The status is verifiable or plausible, so the claim of selection reads as real rather than mass-mailed.; The offer is framed as a continuation of the existing relationship, not a fresh cold pitch.
techniques.dilutes_when: The identity is vague or invented ('because you're a savvy shopper'), so it reads as filler.; Everyone obviously qualifies, which exposes the 'selection' as an untargeted blast.; The claimed relationship is one the reader does not actually recognize or value.; Hard selling immediately swamps the framing, breaking the warm-continuation tone it set up.

techniques.name: Place Identity Fusion
techniques.lede: Place Identity Fusion ties a named physical place to a way of being, so that choosing the product reads as claiming a self.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy names a place, a region, a city, a neighborhood, a landmark, or a home, then defines it as a set of personal traits rather than a set of coordinates. The place stops being a location and becomes a description of the reader: the values, habits, and temperament of anyone who belongs there. Buying, visiting, or owning becomes the way a person joins that description. The product turns into the entry ticket to a self the place already stands for.
techniques.why_it_works: People carry a running answer to who am I, and places are among the cheapest and most stable answers available. A city or a landscape already has an agreed character in the reader's head, built by decades of film, news, and family story, so the copy never has to argue the trait list into existence. It only has to attach the reader to it. Belonging also feels earned rather than bought, which lets a purchase pass as a statement of character instead of a transaction. Identity claims resist counterargument in a way product claims do not.
techniques.lands_when: The place already carries a settled character the reader can name unaided, so the copy borrows meaning instead of building it.; The trait list is specific enough to exclude someone, because a place that flatters everybody describes nobody.; The product plausibly comes from, belongs to, or is used in that place, so the link survives a skeptical reading.; The buyer wants to be seen a certain way by…
techniques.dilutes_when: The place is named but never converted into traits, leaving a provenance stamp that does no identity work.; The traits listed are generic goods like quality and care, which any place could claim and no reader can picture.; The brand has no real tie to the place, so the claim reads as costume and invites the obvious question.; The place carries meanings the buyer does not want, and the copy inheri…

techniques.name: Future-Tense Identity Address
techniques.lede: The copy names the reader by the person they are becoming rather than the person they are, with the future marker doing the work.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy picks a role the reader wants and hands it to them, with a word like future, next, or some day attached so the claim stays honest. Someone who would not yet call themselves a homeowner or an entrepreneur can accept future homeowner or future entrepreneur without arguing. The label is usually a role name, though it can be a described condition instead. It can be a plain address or an instruction to think from that self.
techniques.why_it_works: Self-description is where a lot of persuasion stalls. Tell someone they are a founder and they check the claim against their bank balance and throw it out. The future marker removes the check, because a claim about who you will be cannot be tested today. What stays is the label, now attached to the reader, along with the small commitment that comes with accepting it. Reading on becomes consistent with the identity just granted rather than a decision that has to be argued for, so the offer that follows starts from agreement instead of resistance.
techniques.lands_when: The reader wants the role but would flinch at being called it today, so the softened version is the only one they can take.; The temporal word is explicit and on the page, since that marker is what separates the move from ordinary flattery.; The role names a state the thing on offer actually moves someone toward, so the label reads as a step rather than a wish.; It arrives before the ask, so the…
techniques.dilutes_when: The audience already holds the label, so putting future in front of it reads as a demotion.; The temporal anchor gets dropped and the line turns into plain praise of who the reader is now.; The future is described for the product, the company, or the world rather than pinned to a person, which is vision talk and not an address.; The distance between the reader's current self and the named self is…

techniques.name: Negative Persona Confrontation
techniques.lede: This move holds up a sharp portrait of the person the reader is turning into if nothing changes, drawn precisely enough that the reader flinches in recognition.
techniques.what_it_does: It paints a specific version of the reader they do not want to be: the future self they are drifting toward, or the current self they have quietly become. The details are exact enough that the reader recognizes their own trajectory in the picture. It works by contrast rather than praise. Instead of describing the pain the reader already feels, or the hero they could grow into, it holds up an unflattering mirror and lets the reader supply the verdict, then quietly points to the exit.
techniques.why_it_works: People will strain harder to avoid becoming an unwanted self than to chase a gain. A concrete picture of an undesired self makes the reader sort themselves away from it, the same reflex that makes us distance from an embarrassing stranger. Because the portrait carries real detail, the reader supplies the recognition, so the judgment feels self-authored instead of imposed. That self-issued verdict, I am becoming this and I refuse, creates motion the writer never had to argue for. The reader then moves away from the picture toward whatever better self the copy offers.
techniques.lands_when: The undesired self is drawn with concrete, recognizable detail, not a vague insult.; The reader can plausibly see themselves already drifting toward the portrait.; A better self or clear exit is offered right after, so the recognition has somewhere to go.; The tone matches how the audience already talks to themselves, so the mirror reads as honest rather than cruel.
techniques.dilutes_when: The portrait is a generic put-down the reader shrugs off as aimed at someone else.; It only stirs current pain without naming a self the reader is turning into.; The scorn lands so hard the reader rejects the writer instead of the portrait.; No path away is offered, so recognition sours into shame or resentment with nowhere to go.

techniques.name: Jargon Calibration
techniques.lede: Speak in the exact words the reader's own world uses, pitched at the level the reader has actually reached, so the copy reads as coming from inside the circle rather than outside it.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy picks its vocabulary by audience rather than by subject. It reaches for words a particular group uses among themselves and sets them at the level the reader already stands on. The handling varies: terms can be dropped in bare and left unexplained, one term can be named and glossed on the spot, or the copy can promise plain words while still using the one term the reader would expect. In each case the vocabulary is doing the sorting, separately from whatever the offer turns out to be.
techniques.why_it_works: Vocabulary works as a fast membership test, and readers run it without being asked to. A term used correctly suggests the writer has stood where the reader stands, which buys more trust than simply claiming to understand them. The level also sorts the audience: a reader who knows the words leans in, and a reader who does not can tell the message is aimed elsewhere. When a term is introduced and explained rather than assumed, the reader is moved up a step, which reads as being let in rather than being sold to.
techniques.lands_when: The words come from how the group actually talks among themselves, not from the product's own spec sheet; The level matches where the reader already stands, so the terms land as recognition rather than as a test they might fail; Any unfamiliar term is either the point of the sentence or explained on the spot, so it never sits there as decoration; The vocabulary carries real content, so stripping…
techniques.dilutes_when: The terms sit above the reader, so the passage reads as a wall of words instead of an invitation; The terms sit below the reader, so a knowledgeable audience hears itself being talked down to; Insider words are sprinkled for flavor while the argument underneath would read exactly the same without them; The copy talks about speaking the customer's language instead of actually speaking it

techniques.name: Category-Callback Wordplay
techniques.lede: This move lifts a phrase the audience already knows by heart and swaps one word for the brand's advantage, so the wit and the superiority claim land in the same beat.
techniques.what_it_does: This move borrows a catchphrase, proverb, jingle, or idiom the whole audience can finish from memory, then drops the brand's differentiator into the key slot. The reader's mind auto-completes the familiar original, notices the substituted word, and reads the swap as both a joke and a claim that this product now owns the category. It rides a phrase the culture already made famous, so the brand inherits recognition it never had to build, and reframes itself as the obvious upgrade to a whole category.
techniques.why_it_works: Finishing a half-heard phrase is automatic and quietly satisfying, so the reader supplies the missing beat and feels the claim as self-generated rather than pushed. Familiarity plus a small surprise is what memory holds onto, which makes the line easy to recall and easy to repeat. The borrowed phrase arrives loaded with cultural meaning the brand did not pay to create, and the single swapped word points straight at the advantage. Done well it says, at almost no cost, that this brand is the category's rightful next step.
techniques.lands_when: The original phrase is common enough that the audience finishes it without any prompting.; The swapped word names a real, specific advantage rather than a vague mood.; The pun reads instantly, with no puzzle the reader has to stop and decode.; The playful tone fits a brand the audience already accepts as informal.
techniques.dilutes_when: The source phrase is too obscure, so the callback lands on nothing and reads as a plain statement.; The substitution is forced and the sentence stops making literal sense.; The wordplay buries the benefit instead of pointing at it.; Every line reaches for a pun, so the wit blurs into noise and nothing stands out.

techniques.name: Class-Secret Knowledge
techniques.lede: Frame the knowledge you are selling as something the rich, the elite, or the professional insider already holds and the ordinary reader has never been let in on.
techniques.what_it_does: It splits the world into two tiers: a moneyed or expert class that holds some method, and everyone else who was never let in. The offer becomes the bridge across that line. By attaching the information to a class the reader admires, the copy makes the knowledge feel proven, because the successful already use it, and scarce, because ordinary people do not have it, at the same time. The pull is aspiration plus exclusion: you want what they have, and you resent standing outside it.
techniques.why_it_works: Two drives fire together. Aspiration says the habits of the wealthy or the expert are worth copying, so a method they rely on carries borrowed proof without a single statistic. Exclusion says a line has been drawn and the reader is on the wrong side of it, which stings and demands action. Because the gate is a social class rather than a price tag, crossing it feels like joining rather than buying. The reader is not told the product is good; the reader is told that people they envy already know, and that alone reframes the purchase as catching up.
techniques.lands_when: The copy names a specific higher tier (the rich, insiders, top professionals) and marks the reader as currently outside it.; The knowledge itself, not mere access or membership, is what the class is said to hold.; The gap invites the reader to cross over into the class rather than only admire it from a distance.; The class named is one the reader genuinely aspires to join or quietly envies.
techniques.dilutes_when: The 'insiders' are a vague crowd with no wealth or status marker, so the frame is ordinary social proof.; The pitch gates access or membership but never claims any withheld knowledge.; The elite reference is decoration, dropped once and never tied to what the reader will actually learn.; The knowledge is framed as banned or taboo rather than class-held, which is a different move.

techniques.name: Emotional Reservoir Bridge
techniques.lede: The copy grabs a strong feeling the reader already carries and steers that charge straight toward the offer.
techniques.what_it_does: Rather than building an emotion from scratch, this move reaches for a charge the reader is already carrying: a firm conviction about health, faith, family, or a loss they still feel, and wires that live current to the offer. The copy names the loaded subject early, lets the reader's own belief do the heating, then lays a short path from that heat to the thing being sold. The feeling arrives pre-loaded, so the copy lands fast and needs no warm-up.
techniques.why_it_works: Cold readers give a message a second or two before deciding whether to care, and manufacturing feeling inside that window is slow and easy to resist. Borrowing a feeling the reader already holds is neither slow nor resisted: the conviction is theirs, so it clears the guard a stranger's claim would trip. Once a charged belief is active, the mind looks for somewhere to send it, and the offer stands right there as the outlet. The reader feels understood rather than sold, because the opening began inside their own worldview.
techniques.lands_when: The tapped belief is one the target audience genuinely holds strongly, not one the writer merely wishes they held.; The charged subject is named plainly and early, before the reader has filed the message under 'another pitch'.; The bridge from feeling to offer is short and believable, so the redirect never reads as a bait and switch.; The product can honestly act as an outlet for the emotion, so…
techniques.dilutes_when: The emotion is manufactured on the spot instead of borrowed, which reads as pushy and invites resistance.; The belief tapped is niche or misjudged, so most readers feel nothing or feel talked past.; The leap from the loaded subject to the offer is long or forced, and the reader senses being handled.; The opener leans so hard on the charged topic that it never reaches the product, and the heat sim…

techniques.name: Bundled-Human-Service Naming
techniques.lede: Naming the person who comes with the product, so a job title becomes part of what the buyer is buying.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy gives the bundled human a job title and hangs that title on the product, so the person reads as part of what the buyer gets rather than as after-sales help. The title can carry a real credential, an invented company rank, or a friendly nickname. Some versions add a possessive so the person belongs to the reader. The shape varies, from a one line ownership claim to a short paragraph explaining who picks up and what it costs.
techniques.why_it_works: A product is an object, and any rival can offer a similar object. A named person is harder to copy and easier to picture, so moving the human into the offer changes what the buyer thinks is on the table. When the title carries a credential, the trust already attached to that profession transfers to the purchase. When it carries no credential, the naming still does work: an unnamed help desk sounds like an expense the company would rather avoid, while a titled role sounds like a specific someone who is answerable to you.
techniques.lands_when: The role named is one buyers already trust in the wider world, such as a therapist or a licensed prescriber.; The human is genuinely part of the purchase rather than a paid upgrade sold later.; The title is concrete enough to picture, so the reader knows who will actually pick up.; The category normally ships with no help at all, which makes the person the real point of difference.
techniques.dilutes_when: The role is vague, such as our team or our specialists, and could describe any company's help desk.; The title is invented for the ad and carries no training, licence, or duty a reader could check.; The named person turns out to be a sales step or a bot, so the title promises more than it delivers.; The wording sits only beside the buy button, where it reads as a free consultation offer rather th…

techniques.name: Precision Audience Signal
techniques.lede: Name the exact reader so sharply that the right person feels singled out and everyone else knows to move on.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy calls out a narrow slice of people by a specific trait, situation, age, job, or mindset. Instead of speaking to anyone, it speaks to one kind of person and lets the words do the sorting. The matching reader feels recognized and leans in; the non-matching reader steps aside without being pushed. The naming itself is the persuasive work, because the sharpness of the description signals that whoever wrote it already understands this reader's exact spot.
techniques.why_it_works: People scan for themselves first and decide in a heartbeat whether a message is meant for them. A precise marker answers that question instantly and flatters the reader by implying the sender knows their situation well enough to describe it. The exclusion is a feature, not a cost: by waving off the wrong people, the line raises the felt relevance and trust of the right ones. A reader who thinks this is about me lowers their guard and reads on, and being singled out from a crowd carries its own quiet pull.
techniques.lands_when: The named marker is narrow enough that the wrong reader clearly recognizes it is not for them; The trait described is one the reader privately uses to define themselves; The precision implies real knowledge of the reader's circumstance, not a guess; The rest of the message pays off the promise implied by singling that reader out
techniques.dilutes_when: The marker is so broad that nearly everyone qualifies, so no one feels chosen; The line slides into describing the product's custom features instead of naming the reader; Several audiences are named at once, blurring the sense of a single intended person; The specific tag is decorative and the real claim sits elsewhere in the copy

techniques.name: The Felt-Sense Description
techniques.lede: Put the reader back inside the felt, interior experience of their own situation, not the symptoms of it but the way it feels from within.
techniques.what_it_does: It renders the inside of a situation the way the reader actually lives it: the tightening in the chest, the racing mind, the quiet sense of being unseen, the feeling of being trapped by your own habits. Instead of naming a problem from the outside or listing symptoms, the copy reaches for the emotional and bodily texture of being there. The reader does not just recognize the description as accurate. They feel themselves re-enter the moment, because the words match the private experience they have never quite put into language themselves.
techniques.why_it_works: People trust language that knows how their inside feels. A symptom list reads as observation; a rendered felt sense reads as recognition, and recognition lowers the guard a sales pitch normally raises. When copy names the texture of an experience the reader assumed was private or hard to articulate, it earns the standing of someone who has been there. That borrowed intimacy makes the later promise credible: a writer who can describe the ache this precisely is presumed to understand the cure. The move converts attention into the felt sense of being understood.
techniques.lands_when: The words render an interior or bodily texture the reader recognizes as their own private experience; It reaches past naming a symptom into how the situation actually feels from inside; The reader thinks 'that is exactly it' before any product or fix is mentioned; The texture is specific enough to feel observed rather than guessed
techniques.dilutes_when: It only lists symptoms or problems without rendering the inner feeling of them; It describes the taste, smell, or feel of a product instead of the reader's own situation; It slaps a bare feeling label on the reader ('you're stressed') with no texture behind it; It states a hidden problem as a flat diagnosis rather than as lived experience

techniques.name: Subculture Vocabulary Appropriation
techniques.lede: The copy picks up a word that lives inside a particular group, uses it the way that group uses it, and never stops to explain it.
techniques.what_it_does: A brand picks up a term that circulates inside a specific group, a sport, a scene, a fandom, a clinical community, and drops it into the copy with no definition and no apology. The word arrives as if the writer were already inside. Readers who know it register the brand as one of their own before they read a single claim. Readers who do not know it skim past or quietly conclude the message was not addressed to them, and that loss is accepted as the price of the signal.
techniques.why_it_works: Shared words are the cheapest proof of belonging people have. Picking up a group's vocabulary correctly takes time spent inside the group, so correct use reads as evidence of time served. Explaining the term flips the signal, because a speaker who defines a word is standing outside it and talking to visitors. Using it plainly flatters the reader by assuming fluency, and that flattery lands before any argument about the product starts. The reader's own flash of recognition supplies the endorsement, so the brand never has to claim membership out loud.
techniques.lands_when: The term is used the way the group actually uses it, in the right setting and with the right grammar around it.; The audience is narrow enough that the people who miss the word were never going to buy anyway.; The word is still live inside the group rather than a phrase that already leaked into everybody's feed.; The surrounding sentences keep the same register, so the borrowed word is not sittin…
techniques.dilutes_when: The term gets defined, put in scare quotes, or nudged with a wink, which tells the group a visitor wrote this.; The word is used slightly wrong, which announces outsider status louder than saying nothing would have.; The vocabulary is lifted from a group the brand has no stake in, so recognition curdles into resentment.; Several borrowed terms pile into one line until the voice reads as a costume…

techniques.name: Taboo Rebranded as Goals
techniques.lede: Taboo-as-goals euphemism renames an embarrassing or shameful subject in the upbeat vocabulary of self-improvement, so the reader can act on it without feeling exposed.
techniques.what_it_does: It takes a topic people find awkward to name out loud, such as sexual health, incontinence, body odor, mental illness, or addiction, and re-describes it using words the reader already uses comfortably for ambition: goals, routine, care, regimen, performance, optimization. The subject itself does not change; only the frame does. By borrowing the language of a domain the audience feels good about, the copy invites them to treat the taboo as one more thing they are actively working on rather than something to hide.
techniques.why_it_works: Shame makes people avoid a topic, and avoiding the topic means never buying the fix. When the same need is dressed in achievement language, the reader quietly relocates it from the file of things to be embarrassed about into the file of things being worked on. Goals framing implies agency and progress, which feels active instead of deficient. It also hands the reader a socially acceptable way to describe the purchase to themselves and to others. The euphemism never denies the taboo; it re-files it under a self-image the reader is proud to claim.
techniques.lands_when: The topic carries real social stigma, so the reader needs cover before engaging at all.; The borrowed vocabulary is one the audience genuinely uses for other, prouder pursuits.; The reframe still points clearly at the underlying need, so the reader knows what is being sold.; The achievement frame implies the reader has agency and can make visible progress.
techniques.dilutes_when: The euphemism drifts so far from the subject that readers cannot tell what the product treats.; The borrowed language is corporate jargon the audience does not actually speak.; The tone turns clinical, which reintroduces the very distance the reframe was meant to close.; The wink is so heavy that it points attention back at the shame it was supposed to cover.

techniques.name: Archetype Label Callout
techniques.lede: Name a recognizable type of person in a line or two and let readers slot themselves into the label.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy presents one or more named types, each sketched in a line or two, so a reader scanning them stops at the one that fits. Instead of describing a product or a problem in the abstract, it hands the reader a mirror with a name on it. The naming does the sorting: a person who sees a label that matches their habits, fears, or role feels singled out and read, and keeps reading to find out what the writer knows about their kind.
techniques.why_it_works: People are quick to recognize themselves in a sharp label and slow to resist one that feels accurate. A named type flatters the reader with the sense of being understood, and it turns a broad pitch into a private one: the message now seems written for a specific kind of person, and the reader has just confirmed they are that kind. Self-sorting also builds small commitment. Once a reader accepts the label, the claims that follow inherit its authority, because rejecting them would mean rejecting a self-description they just endorsed.
techniques.lands_when: The label is specific enough that the right reader feels named and the wrong one keeps scrolling.; Each type is drawn in a line or two with concrete habits, not vague adjectives.; The named type connects directly to what the copy goes on to promise or sell.; The reader is offered a real choice among types rather than one label forced on everyone.
techniques.dilutes_when: The label is so broad it fits everyone, so no one feels singled out.; The description lists traits with no behavior a reader can recognize in themselves.; The naming is used to insult rather than to invite, and the reader refuses the tag.; Too many types are stacked at once, and the reader sorts into none of them.

techniques.name: Concierge-Wrapper Positioning
techniques.lede: Sell the same commodity everyone sells, then make the service around it the reason to buy from you.
techniques.what_it_does: It takes a core good that is identical to what every competitor offers, a brand-name drug the seller does not make, off-the-shelf gear, a dropshipped device, an insurance-covered product, and layers a branded, high-touch service experience on top. The copy names that wrapper as the differentiator: a dedicated human advisor, provider-led care, done-for-you paperwork, a personal shopper, a private concierge. The product is conceded to be a commodity, sometimes openly, so the persuasion shifts entirely to how you will be looked after once you buy.
techniques.why_it_works: When the core good is interchangeable, price is the only axis left, and price is a losing fight. Wrapping the commodity in service moves the contest to ground the buyer cannot easily comparison-shop: attention, ease, and the feeling of being personally handled. A named human or a done-for-you promise also reduces the anxiety of a purchase the buyer feels unqualified to make alone. The buyer stops weighing the product, which is settled, and starts weighing the experience, which the seller controls and competitors cannot quickly copy.

techniques.name: Identity-Mirror Positioning
techniques.lede: The seller claims to be the same kind of person as the buyer, compressing that shared identity into one positioning line: for people like us, by people like us.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy names the buyer's identity or stance, then claims the seller holds exactly the same one. The classic shape is the paired formula, by X for X, but the move also shows up as a first person confession (I am one of you) or a team description (built by people who live this). It does not argue the product is better; it argues the maker is the buyer, so the product must already fit. One short line carries the entire position.
techniques.why_it_works: Buyers arrive wary of the category, and that wariness is aimed at outsiders selling in. When the seller adopts the buyer's own identity, the line dissolves the divide that suspicion needs; someone counted as one of us gets the benefit of the doubt reserved for the in-group, what Cialdini calls unity. The claim also implies built-in competence: a maker who shares your situation already knows the requirements you would have to explain to anyone else. And it flatters, because your identity was worth building a company around.

techniques.dilutes_when: The mirrored identity is generic (busy people, ambitious professionals), so no reader feels specifically named.; The maker plainly does not share the trait, which turns the mirror into a trust liability the moment buyers check.; The line gets stretched into a long origin narrative; the power here is compression, and a full story persuades by different means.; Several identities are mirrored at on…

techniques.name: Disqualification Gate
techniques.lede: Copy that turns the wrong reader away on purpose, so the readers who stay feel chosen instead of chased.
techniques.what_it_does: It builds a gate into the message. Instead of widening the door to let everyone in, the copy names the people it does not want and tells them to leave: do not read this, do not buy this, stop here unless you meet the bar. The bar can be a price, a required action, a level of seriousness, or a trait the reader must lack. Everyone who reads past the gate has, in effect, raised a hand and put themselves on the inside of the line the copy just drew.
techniques.why_it_works: Rejection is a stronger signal of value than welcome. When a seller pushes people away, the reader reads it as confidence: this thing is real enough that it can afford to lose buyers. The act of self-selecting past the screen turns a passive prospect into someone who has already decided they belong, so the later ask meets a reader who feels picked rather than pitched. It also flatters by contrast. Naming the people who fail the screen lets the reader place themselves above that group, and few of us volunteer to be the ones who were not good enough.
techniques.lands_when: The screen is concrete: a real price, a real action, or a clearly named trait the reader can check themselves against.; The disqualified group is one the target reader actively does not want to be lumped in with.; The turn-away is sincere enough that staying feels like a choice the reader made, not a trick the seller ran.; The offer behind the gate can actually deliver to the people who pass, so…
techniques.dilutes_when: The copy only describes its ideal customer and never tells anyone to leave, which is a label, not a gate.; Everyone passes the screen, so the exclusion is theater and the reader senses it.; The bar is vague flattery ('for serious people') with no test a reader can fail.; The rejection reads as contempt for the audience rather than respect for the few, and the reader walks for real.

techniques.name: Tribal Marker
techniques.lede: Plant a reference only the right people will catch, and recognition itself becomes the membership card.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy drops a specific in-joke, coined member name, or piece of insider jargon that the intended audience decodes instantly and everyone else reads right past. It does not explain the reference. The reader who gets it feels seen and sorted into the group; the reader who does not is quietly filtered out. Comprehension becomes the test of belonging, and the brand earns trust by proving it speaks the audience's private language rather than the flattened language of mass marketing.
techniques.why_it_works: People extend trust faster to those who already share their world, and a correctly placed insider signal is hard to fake, so it reads as proof of real membership rather than a pitch. The reader does the work of recognizing the reference, and that small act of decoding feels like self-discovery, not selling. Being addressed in one's own dialect flatters identity and creates a quick us-feeling. The deliberate exclusion of outsiders also raises the value of being inside, so the right reader leans in precisely because not everyone is meant to.
techniques.lands_when: The reference is specific enough that an outsider cannot fake it, so getting it certifies real membership; The audience is a defined subculture with its own vocabulary, rituals, or shared experiences to draw on; The signal stays unexplained, letting the reader earn the recognition instead of being handed it; The brand has standing to use the language, so it reads as a peer speaking, not a markete…
techniques.dilutes_when: The reference is explained or glossed, which turns a membership test into a plain statement anyone can read; The signal is so broad that everyone recognizes it, so it no longer sorts anyone in or out; The jargon is misused or dated, marking the brand as a poser to the very group it courts; A louder move carries the line, such as a stated belief, an enemy to rally against, or a direct salutation,…

techniques.name: Negative Attribute Differentiation
techniques.lede: Win the category by loudly featuring what your product leaves out.
techniques.what_it_does: This move turns an absence into the main claim. Instead of stacking up features, the copy names one or more ingredients, parts, or practices that the category is known for and that buyers quietly resent, then declares the product free of them. No additive, no hidden fee, no engine to maintain, no fabricated answer. The absence becomes the reason to choose. It reframes the comparison around what the product leaves out, so the brand stops competing on the usual scorecard and starts owning the gap everyone else has to defend.
techniques.why_it_works: Buyers carry a standing objection about a category before they ever read your copy. Naming the thing they distrust and then removing it answers the worry before it can harden into a reason to walk away. Absence is also easy to verify and hard to fake, so a clean negative reads as more honest than another superlative. It sorts the market into us and them without naming a rival, letting the reader supply the villains from memory. And a single subtraction is easier to remember than a list of additions.
techniques.lands_when: The absence names the category's best-known objection, not a random missing part.; The thing left out is something rivals cannot easily drop themselves.; The negative is concrete and checkable, so the claim feels like proof.; One sharp subtraction carries the line instead of a long compliance list.
techniques.dilutes_when: The absence list is generic table stakes everyone already claims.; The missing attribute is one nobody actually worried about.; The line slides into attacking a named rival instead of owning its own gap.; So many negatives pile up that no single one is memorable.

techniques.name: Tradition Appeal
techniques.lede: Tradition Appeal frames a purchase as stepping into a long, proud lineage the reader can be honored to carry forward.
techniques.what_it_does: This move casts a product, brand, or choice as part of an established custom that reaches back through generations. It names a heritage, a time-honored practice, or an unbroken line of people who came before, then holds a place in that line open for the reader. The offer stops being a plain transaction and becomes an act of continuity: to buy is to honor, join, and carry forward something older and larger than any single season or sale.
techniques.why_it_works: People trust what has lasted. A practice that survives generations reads as tested, safe, and worth belonging to, so tradition borrows the authority of time without having to argue a single point. It also flatters, because joining a proud lineage confers identity and standing with the discerning few who still value the old ways. And it lowers felt risk. Choosing the time-honored option feels responsible rather than reckless, since countless others chose it before and the custom still endures today.
techniques.lands_when: The lineage is real and specific enough to picture, not a vague gesture at heritage; The audience already prizes continuity, craft, or belonging over novelty; The tradition connects to the product's actual substance, not just its packaging; The reader is invited to join and carry it forward, not only admire it from outside
techniques.dilutes_when: The heritage is invented or borrowed and the claim collapses under a moment's scrutiny; Tradition is asserted as a bare label with no custom, story, or lineage behind it; The audience wants the newer and better option, so age reads as stale rather than proven; Every rival makes the same timeless claim, so the lineage stops distinguishing anything

techniques.name: Identity-Binding Salutation
techniques.lede: Open by hailing the reader as a kind of person, not by name.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy begins with a salutation aimed at an identity: a trait, a role, a tribe, or a self-description the reader either claims or rejects on the spot. Instead of 'Dear customer' or a first name, it says 'To the obsessed,' 'For the people who build,' 'Calling all founders.' The form does two jobs at once. It filters, because anyone who does not see themselves in the label reads past and leaves. And it bonds, because anyone who does see themselves feels named, chosen, and spoken to directly before a single claim is made.
techniques.why_it_works: People pay attention to messages addressed to who they are, not to everyone. A salutation built on identity skips the usual work of earning interest, because the reader supplies the interest by recognizing themselves. The label also flatters: being singled out as one of a named few feels better than being one of a crowd. And once a reader silently agrees 'yes, that is me,' they have made a small commitment that the rest of the copy can build on. The self-deselection is a feature, not a loss, since it concentrates the message on the people most likely to act.
techniques.lands_when: The opening word or line is a salutation aimed at an identity the target reader proudly claims.; The named identity is specific enough that some readers clearly fall outside it.; The claimed label flatters or dignifies the reader rather than merely describing a market segment.; The bond is set before any pitch, so the reader is already inside the tent when the offer arrives.
techniques.dilutes_when: The label is so broad ('Dear valued customer') that no one feels singled out and no one self-deselects.; The identity is named in the body or a tagline but never opens the piece as a true salutation.; The copy describes a third-party character or villain instead of addressing the reader.; The claimed identity rings false or pandering, so the named reader rejects the flattery.

techniques.name: Belief Echo
techniques.lede: Belief Echo says the reader's current belief back to them, in their own words, before it tries to move them anywhere.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy names a belief the reader already holds and states it plainly, without arguing with it. It can be a private suspicion, a piece of received wisdom, a worry the reader has never said out loud, or the exact sentence they say to themselves. The statement comes first and stands on its own. Only after the reader has recognized their own position does the copy add to it, confirm it, or turn it. The order is the technique: echo first, then move.
techniques.why_it_works: Being described accurately reads as being understood. A reader who sees their own belief written down concludes the writer has stood where they stand, which buys the writer the right to say what comes next. The echo also lowers the reader's guard, because there is nothing to push back on in a sentence they already agree with, so agreement accumulates before any claim arrives. And once the belief sits on the page instead of in the reader's head, it can be confirmed or overturned in the open rather than quietly resisting every line that follows.
techniques.lands_when: The belief is written in the reader's own plain words, close to how they would say it to a friend.; It is a belief the reader actually holds today, not one the writer wishes they held.; The echo arrives before the pitch, so the reader agrees with something before being asked for anything.; The belief is specific enough that the reader thinks the writer has met people like them.
techniques.dilutes_when: The belief is a strawman, so the reader reads it and thinks that is not what I think.; The writer states the brand's belief instead of the reader's, which asks for trust rather than earning it.; The echo is overruled in the same breath, so it reads as a setup rather than a hearing.; The belief is so broad that agreeing with it costs nothing and proves nothing about the writer.

techniques.name: Coined Category with Etymology
techniques.lede: A made-up name for a discipline, followed at once by a definition that fixes what it means, so the invention arrives sounding like a field of study.
techniques.what_it_does: The writer names something that did not have a name before, usually a stitched-together word with a technical or Latin feel. Then, without a beat, the copy gives the word its charter: what it means, what it draws on, or what it covers. The definition does the persuading. A reader who would shrug at a slogan slows down for something that looks like a dictionary entry, and the invented word starts behaving like an established term.
techniques.why_it_works: An unpacked word reads as a word somebody had to earn. Dictionaries, textbooks and course catalogs all use this same shape, so borrowing the shape borrows the standing that comes with it, and the reader grants the term a history it does not have. The breakdown also converts a claim into a category. Once a buyer accepts the field, the seller is the only one working in it, and every rival gets measured against a yardstick the seller wrote. Nothing has been proven, yet the ground has quietly moved.
techniques.lands_when: The parts being unpacked are real and checkable, so the breakdown survives a reader looking each piece up.; The invented name covers something the buyer already feels but has never had a word for.; The unpacking stays short, two or three components, rather than a wall of vocabulary.; Everything after it works inside the new field instead of drifting back to ordinary product claims.
techniques.dilutes_when: The roots are decorative, so the breakdown collapses the moment anyone tests it.; The coined name is only a rebadge of a plain word buyers already use comfortably.; Every feature in the line gets its own coined name, so no single one carries weight.; The definition runs long and technical, and the reader loses the promise while parsing the vocabulary.

techniques.name: Creator Role Invitation
techniques.lede: An action command that hands the reader a maker's identity, so choosing the product feels like becoming someone rather than buying something.
techniques.what_it_does: Imperative Self Cast opens with a verb of doing, build, create, broadcast, become, and aims it straight at the reader. The grammar skips past the sale and installs the reader in an active role: creator, contributor, member, doer. Instead of describing what a product is, it tells the reader what they will make or who they will be. The command carries an implied identity, and accepting the command means accepting the identity. Adoption then reads as self-expression, not a transaction to be resisted.
techniques.why_it_works: A command in the second person casts the reader as the subject of the action, not its target. People resist being sold to, but rarely resist a picture of themselves in motion. By naming a doing role, build, serve, create, the copy lets the reader try on an identity at no cost, and the identity does the persuading. It also flatters agency: the reader, not the brand, appears to be the one making things happen. Once someone pictures themselves as a maker, the product becomes the obvious tool for the person they already imagine being.
techniques.lands_when: The verb names a real creative or contributing act the reader can picture doing.; The identity on offer flatters the reader's existing self-image or ambition.; The product genuinely lets the reader make or shape something, so the cast pays off.; The command stays short and confident, reading as an invitation rather than an order.
techniques.dilutes_when: The imperative is a generic buy or click, casting no identity beyond customer.; The role promised is far grander than anything the product actually enables.; Commands pile up until the reader feels ordered around instead of invited in.; The doing verb is vague, like engage or leverage, and conjures no concrete act.

techniques.name: The Secret Society Frame
techniques.lede: Tell the reader they belong to a small, knowing circle that has access to what everyone else is locked out of.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy draws a line between a select few and everyone else, then places the reader on the inside. It names an in-group (members, insiders, the well-connected, the savvy few) and signals that what follows is shared only among that circle. Outsiders are pushed away, sometimes explicitly told this is not for them. The reader is invited to step through a door most people never find, and the pull is the membership itself, not just the information behind the door.
techniques.why_it_works: Belonging is a deep social drive, and exclusion is its lever. When copy implies a closed circle of people who know more, earn more, or live better, the reader wants to be inside it rather than left out with the crowd. The frame flatters: choosing to read already marks you as one of the few. It borrows the prestige of the in-group and transfers it to the offer, so accepting the offer feels like claiming a status, not making a purchase. Scarcity of membership makes the knowledge feel more valuable than the same facts offered to everyone.
techniques.lands_when: The copy names a bounded in-group and clearly places the reader inside it; Outsiders are drawn as a contrast, the many who never hear about this; Membership or access, not just the secret's contents, carries the persuasion; The reader feels chosen or qualified simply by reading on
techniques.dilutes_when: The real spine is a hidden truth suppressed by a named enemy, which is a different move; A bare statistic like 99 percent or top 1 percent does the work as a number, not a circle; It only teases a withheld fact to force a click, with no in-group identity; Everyone is invited, so there is no select few and no inside to join

techniques.name: Situational Qualifier
techniques.lede: A line that names one narrow circumstance, season, or stage of life, so the reader who is standing in it knows the message was written for them.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy names a situation rather than a person: a usage level, a time of year, a point in a career, a moment in the day. The reader checks that description against their own life and either steps forward or steps aside. Nothing has been claimed about the product yet. The line is doing sorting work, marking out who the argument that follows is aimed at, and it does that by staying narrow enough that most readers can answer yes or no without thinking twice.
techniques.why_it_works: People skim until something describes them. A broad label like busy parents or small business owners is easy to read past, because it fits too many people to feel personal. A tight circumstance is harder to ignore, since recognizing yourself in it feels like being addressed by name. The narrowness also carries a quiet proof claim: whoever wrote this has met people in this exact spot, so they probably understand the rest of it. Readers outside the description leave on their own, which raises the quality of everyone who stays.
techniques.lands_when: The circumstance is narrow enough that a reader can answer yes or no in a second, with no guessing.; The detail is one the reader would use to describe their own life, not a label the seller invented.; What follows genuinely depends on that circumstance, so the sorting line earns its place.; The people it turns away are people the offer really cannot serve.
techniques.dilutes_when: The circumstance is so wide it covers almost everyone, so it reads as filler.; Qualifiers are stacked until the reader stops checking each one and starts skimming.; The named situation has nothing to do with what the product actually does.; The wording comes from the seller's category language rather than the words the reader uses.

techniques.name: Master Plan as Strategy Artifact
techniques.lede: A company's operating strategy is published as a document in its own right, a short sequence of steps the reader is handed and can hold the writer to later.
techniques.what_it_does: The writer states in public the order the business intends to run in: what gets built first, what that pays for, what follows. Each step is cut to a line or two, so years of work read as a short list. Shapes vary. Some plans are numbered, some name their phases and attach a target to each, some read as a run of standing commitments rather than stages. The document is often given a name, and it is addressed to readers who do not work there.
techniques.why_it_works: Putting the sequence on the record changes what the reader is asked to do. Instead of judging a product, which most readers cannot do well, they judge whether the steps follow from each other, which anyone can. The compression helps: when the whole arc fits in one reading, any single product can be placed inside it. A plan that can be checked later also reads as confidence, since the writer has handed over the measure they will be held to. The reader becomes a witness rather than a prospect.
techniques.lands_when: The steps depend on each other, so each one explains why the next becomes possible.; The person publishing it is the person who will run it, which makes the plan a commitment rather than a forecast.; Every step is short enough that the whole arc can be held in mind at once.; The plan says something a reader could not have worked out from the current product line.
techniques.dilutes_when: The items are goals sitting side by side, so nothing in the list depends on anything else.; Near steps and distant steps get the same amount of detail, which hides how little of it is decided.; The plan restates what the company already sells, so publishing it costs the writer nothing.; The wording is loose enough that no later outcome could ever contradict it.

techniques.name: Anti-Basic Frame
techniques.lede: Anti-Basic Frame sorts the reader out of the ordinary crowd, so that choosing this option reads as a sign of taste rather than as a purchase.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy points at the choice most people make and marks it as beneath the reader. Often the ordinary option is named outright, a rival car, a drugstore shelf, a carousel of black suitcases, the crowd itself. Sometimes it is only implied by a claim to taste. Either way the reader is handed a smaller group to belong to, one defined by what it refuses. What is on offer, whether a product or simply a stance, then works as the badge of that refusal.
techniques.why_it_works: Buying is also self-description, and this frame hands the reader a description ready made. Refusing the common option costs nothing, yet it feels like judgment, so the reader gets to be discerning at the price of the item. It also changes the question being asked. Instead of weighing features against features, the reader is asked which kind of person they are, and the ordinary choice now carries a small social cost. Much of the flattery is left for the reader to supply, which is why it can land without sounding like praise.
techniques.lands_when: The ordinary option is common enough that the reader can picture it without being told twice.; The refusal points at something concrete, an object, a habit, or a crowd, rather than just claiming to be different.; The thing being sold really does differ in a way the reader can check on arrival.; The reader already suspects they are not the average buyer, and the copy only confirms it.
techniques.dilutes_when: The copy says it is different without ever saying what it is different from.; The scorn lands on the people who chose the ordinary option rather than on the option itself.; The audience is wide, so writing off the mainstream writes off most of the readers.; Every brand in the category runs the same refusal, which turns the frame into the new ordinary.

techniques.name: The Permission Statement
techniques.lede: The copy tells the reader that what they feel or struggle with is normal and blameless, lowering shame before it asks for anything.
techniques.what_it_does: It names the reader's private struggle, embarrassment, or stalled effort and immediately grants absolution: it is human, it makes sense, it is not your fault. Rather than stirring the wound, the line releases the reader from blame and self-judgment. By removing shame first, it clears the defensiveness that would otherwise block the message. Any pitch that follows arrives to a reader who feels understood and accepted rather than accused, and who is therefore willing to keep reading and to trust the voice doing the reassuring.
techniques.why_it_works: Shame makes people defensive and quick to look away, and a reader braced for judgment does not buy. When the copy says the struggle is normal and blameless, it removes the threat and lowers the guard, and the relief itself lands as a small gift that builds goodwill toward the source. The reader also reads the writer as an ally instead of a critic, which makes every later claim easier to accept. Permission turns a private, isolating problem into a shared, ordinary one that a product can plausibly help with.
techniques.lands_when: The struggle it forgives is one the reader already carries private shame about.; The absolution is explicit: it is okay, it makes sense, it is human, it is not your fault.; It comes before the pitch, so relief precedes the ask.; The voice reads as a peer or ally, not a superior handing down a pardon.
techniques.dilutes_when: It names the shame but amplifies it instead of releasing it, tipping into fear or agitation.; The reassurance is generic comfort with no specific struggle actually being forgiven.; It absolves something the reader never felt guilty about, so there is nothing to relieve.; It is really a mission statement about the company rather than a release for the reader.

techniques.name: Identity-Upgrade Social Proof
techniques.lede: Proof that gets its force from who is already using the thing, with those users named as the kind of person the reader would like to become.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy names the people who have already bought, joined, or worn the thing, and names them by identity rather than by problem. Athletes, founders, arbiters of taste, serious readers, a titled club with a count attached. The reader is not told that the product settles a complaint. The reader is told that a group exists, that the group is worth belonging to, and that buying is the way to get counted inside it. Proof and aspiration arrive in the same sentence.
techniques.why_it_works: Two pressures stack. The first is ordinary crowd evidence: once others have chosen, the choice feels safer and the thinking gets handed off. The second is aspiration, because people copy the sort of person they want to resemble far more readily than they copy strangers, so proof from a flattering reference group outweighs a larger but blander count. Naming the group also hands over a ready-made membership card. The purchase stops being a spending decision and becomes a small act of self-description, which is much harder to argue the reader out of.

techniques.dilutes_when: The adopters are generic ("users", "customers", "people"), so the count proves popularity but flatters nobody.; The identity is asserted about the reader alone, with no other adopters in the frame, which is aspiration rather than proof.; The reference group is admired for something the reader has no wish to be, so the borrowed status has nowhere to land.; The names sit so far above the reader tha…

techniques.name: Commitment-Filter Anti-Guarantee
techniques.lede: The seller takes the refund promise off the table and lets the missing safety net decide who is allowed to buy.
techniques.what_it_does: Most offers lower the risk of saying yes: try it, and if you do not like it, ask for your money back. This move does the opposite. The copy states plainly that there are no refunds, no cancellations, no way back out, and then treats that hard term as the point rather than as fine print. Anyone who needs an exit is told to walk away. Anyone who stays has paid in certainty before paying in money. The terms of sale become the entry test.
techniques.why_it_works: Pulling the escape hatch does several jobs at once. It sorts the audience, because only people who already believe the claim will accept a purchase they cannot undo. It signals confidence, since a seller with a weak product usually hides behind the longest guarantee available. It raises the buyer's own stake, so the purchase feels chosen rather than sampled, and people defend choices they made under their own steam. In a market thick with promises, the refusal also reads as candor, so the missing guarantee lands as honesty instead of as a warning.

techniques.dilutes_when: The seller is unknown and the page shows no other proof, so the missing refund reads as a warning rather than as confidence.; The hard term is softened in the very next line, which drops the filter and leaves only a lost guarantee.; Refunds are required by law or by the selling platform, so the term cannot hold and the rest of the copy loses trust with it.; The product is an ordinary item the buy…

techniques.name: Double-Duty Adjective
techniques.lede: A single word carries two true meanings at once: it names what the product literally is and what the brand stands for, so one reading quietly vouches for the other.
techniques.what_it_does: One ordinary word, whatever its part of speech, sits in a spot where two readings are both accurate. The reader takes in the plain product fact and the brand's stance in the same beat, with no signal that a figure of speech is running. The line looks like a straight description while doing positioning work underneath. Neither sense decorates the other; both are asserted as literally true, which is what separates this from a metaphor that maps one thing onto an unlike thing.
techniques.why_it_works: The reader decodes the second meaning without being handed it, and a meaning you reach yourself sticks harder than one you are told. Because the literal sense is checkably true of the product, the stance rides on that real attribute and feels earned rather than declared. The move also compresses a description and a values pitch into one small unit, which helps recall and reads as wit instead of a sales push. The tiny double-take rewards attention and passes a bit of goodwill to the brand.
techniques.lands_when: The literal sense is plainly, checkably true of the product, so the stance rides on a real attribute rather than a wish; The word lands at a headline or tagline moment where the reader has a beat to catch both meanings; The brand position being claimed is one the company can actually back with evidence or behavior; Both meanings push the same direction, so the pun reinforces the message instead o…
techniques.dilutes_when: Only the clever reading is true and the literal product sense is a stretch, so it reads as a groan; The chosen word drags in a third, unwanted meaning that cuts against the stance; The line needs a caption or a nudge to be understood, which kills the instant recognition; The stance half promises something the product cannot support, turning the wit into overreach
