techniques.name: The Enemy Admission
techniques.lede: A claim lands hardest when it comes out of the mouth of the person who would rather it were not true.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy hands its central claim to someone standing on the other side: a competitor, a critic, a regulator, a former opponent, a rival expert. Then it shows that party conceding. The concession can be a printed quote, a court record, a trade journal, a public filing, or a move made against their own interest. The seller stops asserting and starts reporting. What the reader receives is not the company's opinion of itself but the other side's, given up unwillingly and on the record.
techniques.why_it_works: Readers price every claim by the motive of whoever makes it. Praise from a friendly source gets discounted automatically, because the speaker gains by saying it. A hostile source gains nothing and often loses something, so the usual discount has nowhere to go and the statement reads as fact rather than sales talk. It also closes an argument the reader was already having privately. The objection they were preparing gets raised by the very people best placed to raise it, and then dropped by those same people, in their own words.
techniques.lands_when: The conceding party is visibly on the other side and the reader already knows whose side that is.; The admission is quoted or cited with a name, a date, or a record the reader could go check.; What gets conceded is the exact claim being sold, not a vague compliment nearby.; The concession costs the speaker something real: money, standing, or a position they defended in public.
techniques.dilutes_when: The named opponent means nothing to the reader, so no one has given anything up.; The quote is paraphrased or unsourced, which turns a record into gossip.; Silence is dressed up as agreement, as when nobody has actually admitted anything and the copy claims their quiet says it all.; The admission is buried in a stack of friendly endorsements until it reads as one more testimonial.

techniques.name: Why-There-Not-Here Curiosity
techniques.lede: A named faraway place where something impossible is normal, framed so the reader has to ask why it happens there and not at home.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy names a specific distant location and ties an anomaly to it: a disease that never strikes, people who live impossibly long, a remedy found nowhere else. The geography does two jobs at once. Naming a real place makes the claim feel like reported fact rather than a sales pitch, and an effect bound to one spot on the map implies a hidden, discoverable cause. The reader wants that cause, so they keep going to learn what the far-off place knows.
techniques.why_it_works: A specific place-name reads as reportable fact, not advertising, so skepticism drops before it forms. An effect tied to a single location begs for an explanation, and that open question pulls attention forward until it is answered. Distance adds romance and plausible secrecy: if the cause were nearby, we would already know it, so remoteness explains why the reader has never heard this before. The frame also borrows the authority of discovery and travel reporting, casting the seller as the one who went there and carried the answer back.
techniques.lands_when: The place is specific and checkable, not a vague gesture at somewhere overseas.; The anomaly genuinely defies expectation, so the why-there question feels worth asking.; The copy withholds the cause long enough to hold the loop open.; The eventual payoff connects that far-off cause to something the reader can do or buy.
techniques.dilutes_when: The location is generic or invented, so the reader senses a stage set instead of a report.; The claimed effect is ordinary, giving no reason to wonder why that place is special.; The cause is handed over in the same breath, closing the gap before curiosity forms.; The exotic origin is buried under so many other marvels that nothing feels like a single discoverable secret.

techniques.name: The Paradigm Shift Frame
techniques.lede: The move that changes the question, resetting how the reader thinks about a whole field so the product becomes the obvious answer.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy stops arguing the product on the old terms and redraws the map instead. It proposes a new way of understanding an entire field: what the real problem is, what era we are now in, what the rules have become. Once the reader accepts the new frame, the old options look obsolete and the product sits at the center of the new picture as the natural choice. It sells the worldview first and the product second, so agreement arrives before any single claim is tested.
techniques.why_it_works: People resist a sales pitch but rarely resist a fresh way of seeing. A pitch invites counterargument; a frame reorganizes the ground the argument stands on. When the reader adopts a new model of the domain, they discard the old options on their own, without being told to, and the product arrives as a conclusion they feel they reached themselves. The reframe also flatters: accepting the new lens makes the reader feel early, informed, ahead of a crowd still thinking the old way. The frame does the persuading before the offer is ever weighed.
techniques.lands_when: The new frame names a whole domain, not just the product, so the shift reads as insight rather than a slogan.; The old model is stated plainly enough that the reader recognizes their own current thinking in it.; The product falls out of the new frame as the obvious next step, not as a separate ask bolted on afterward.; The reframe carries a reason to believe, a change already underway, so it read…
techniques.dilutes_when: The 'new way' is only a fresh label on the same product, with no real change to how the reader thinks.; The copy declares a new era but never says what actually changed, so it is a time stamp, not a model.; The old frame is attacked but no replacement is offered, leaving the reader with nothing to adopt.; Feature talk crowds the frame, so the reframe becomes decoration on an ordinary benefit list.

techniques.name: Don't X, Do Y Repositioning
techniques.lede: Name the tired road the whole category walks, cross it out, and hand the reader the different road your offer opens.
techniques.what_it_does: It calls out the default move everyone in the category makes, negates it in plain words, and hands over a substitute path that chases the same goal along a different line. The negation carries the framing: by putting the worn default into words and striking it through, the copy makes the alternative feel like the only sensible option left standing. Everything rides on one clean pivot. Not that well-trodden way, this way instead. The reader is repositioned from the crowd's path onto the one the offer was built to serve.
techniques.why_it_works: People judge a choice against a reference point. Naming the default and rejecting it installs that reference, so the alternative reads as the upgrade rather than just another option. Hearing "don't" grants permission to walk away from a path the reader already half-suspected was a trap, which lowers resistance before the pitch even arrives. The rejection also signals the speaker has traveled the common road and found it wanting, so authority comes for free. And a single either-or pivot is easy to hold in mind, which makes the reframe stick and travel.
techniques.lands_when: The negated path is one the audience genuinely recognizes as the default, so the rejection lands as a real fork in the road.; The alternative is concrete and stays inside the same goal, not a leap to an unrelated promise.; The two halves are tight and parallel, so the pivot from old road to new is felt in a single beat.; The speaker has standing to reject the common path, so the "don't" reads as…
techniques.dilutes_when: The "don't" arrives with no substitute, leaving a complaint instead of a redirection.; The rejected path is a strawman nobody in the audience was actually taking.; The offered alternative is just the same default rebranded, so the fork is fake.; The negation stacks so many "not this, not that" clauses that no single alternative stands out to walk toward.

techniques.name: Loophole Frame
techniques.lede: The Loophole Frame sells an opportunity as a legal exception: a gap in the official rules that lets you do something that sounds forbidden, with permission.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy takes an offer and rebuilds it as an exception to the rules. A named law, code section, provision, or piece of official paper becomes the hero of the pitch: because this rule exists, you can now do the thing that sounds illegal, off limits, or too good to be allowed. The legality language carries the persuasive weight. Words like legal, allowed, mandated, and loophole do the selling, and the product is positioned as the key that fits the gap.
techniques.why_it_works: Forbidden things are attractive, and permission removes the cost of wanting them. The frame delivers both at once: the thrill of getting away with something and the comfort of official blessing. A specific citation borrows the authority of government itself, which answers the too good to be true objection before the reader can raise it. It also flatters the reader as an insider, since a loophole is by definition something most people miss. Part of this is reactance: when a thing was restricted, its release feels newly valuable.
techniques.lands_when: The claim rests on a real, checkable rule, provision, or eligibility gap.; The promised act sounds forbidden or implausible, so the legality claim answers a live objection.; The audience already believes the system quietly favors insiders, as in tax, finance, and offshore markets.; The citation is specific: a named code, section, year, or document the reader could look up.

techniques.name: The Trick Reframe
techniques.lede: The technique relabels a hard-won skill as a mere trick, hack, or secret, so a reader who assumed it took talent suddenly believes it is just a thing to be shown.
techniques.what_it_does: It takes a capability the reader believes is locked behind talent or years of practice and renames it a trick, hack, cheat, or secret. The core move strips the mystique, calling the skill a simple, learnable move rather than a gift; often it also suggests the reader was kept from this easy secret, adding a note of relief and mild grievance. It travels anywhere people assume a skill gap is fixed rather than teachable: memory, math, cooking, selling, investing, fitness.
techniques.why_it_works: Renaming a skill as a trick collapses the distance between where the reader stands and mastery. If greatness is inborn, the reader is shut out for good; if it is a trick, the only thing between them and the result is a piece of information they can go get. The frame also flatters. The reader is not untalented, just uninformed, and someone hid the shortcut from them. That blend of relief, self-forgiveness, and mild grievance lowers resistance and makes a small purchase feel less like a gamble and more like claiming something that was theirs all along.
techniques.lands_when: The skill is one readers truly believe is inborn, such as memory, creativity, or a head for numbers, so the reframe delivers real relief.; The label lands on the capability itself, not just the product, so the promise reads as 'this is learnable' rather than 'buy this thing.'; A short, concrete effort is named, like minutes a day or one simple move, which makes the trick feel real instead of holl…
techniques.dilutes_when: The capability was never seen as talent-gated, so calling it a trick reframes nothing the reader was worried about.; The words 'trick,' 'hack,' and 'secret' pile up until they read as filler rather than a claim.; The trick is named but never made plausible, so it sounds like an empty cheat with nothing behind it.; The reframe promises no shortcut past the exact effort the reader dreads, leaving t…

techniques.name: Occasion Agnostic Claim
techniques.lede: An occasion agnostic claim names several unlike moments a buyer might be in, then says the same product fits all of them, so no moment counts as the wrong one.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy lists contexts that pull against each other, a backyard cookout and a quiet night alone, work and travel, two in the afternoon and two in the morning, and puts one unchanged product inside all of them. The list stays short and concrete, then closes with a phrase that sweeps up the rest: any occasion, anywhere, whatever the weather. Nothing about the product shifts across the contexts. What shifts is the reader's sense of when the thing belongs.
techniques.why_it_works: Most products get quietly filed under one slot: a party drink, a hiking shoe, a Sunday project. The slot decides how often the thing is bought. A reader who already agrees the product is good can still decline on timing, because the moment in front of them is not the moment the product is for. Naming several unlike moments removes that veto before it forms, and the contrast does the work: if it covers both ends, the middle is taken care of. More use situations mean more buying situations.
techniques.lands_when: The named contexts genuinely pull against each other, one casual and one formal, one indoors and one out, so the span is felt rather than asserted.; The product really is the same across all of them, with no separate version or setup needed for each context.; The moments come from the reader's own week, described in recognizable detail rather than as generic categories.; It answers a timing objec…
techniques.dilutes_when: Only the sweeping phrase appears, fit for any occasion, with no actual contexts named, so nothing is actually dissolved.; The listed contexts are all the same kind of moment, which shows a narrow product while claiming a wide one.; The category has a strong slot buyers trust, so claiming every occasion reads as a product unsure what it is.; The stretch reaches a context where the product plainly…

techniques.name: Sovereignty Reframe
techniques.lede: Sovereignty Reframe takes a problem the reader has filed under someone else's control and re-files it under their own, so acting alone becomes the obvious answer rather than a consolation prize.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy often grants that an outside party, an institution, a market, a rival claim on the reader's time, is holding the reader's outcome, and then relabels the problem as the reader's own to solve. Other versions skip that grant and state the sovereign posture directly, as a belief or a right the reader already holds. Either way, once the problem reads as a self-ownership problem, a solo step, a course, a practice, a purchase made alone, reads as the actual fix instead of a substitute for the other party changing.
techniques.why_it_works: People stall when the lever sits in someone else's hand, because waiting becomes the only available move and waiting feels terrible. Naming the lever as theirs turns helplessness into a decision, and that swap is a relief. It also reads as a compliment rather than an accusation, since being told you are the deciding factor credits your capability, provided the copy has already agreed the outside trouble is genuine. And because the restated problem sits inside the reader, an offer they can start alone becomes the only shaped-to-fit answer.
techniques.lands_when: The copy agrees in plain words that the outside problem is real before it moves the problem inward.; The reader is already stuck waiting on a person, a market, or an institution to move first.; What gets handed back is named concretely, the pace, the price, the terms, the shape of the day, not just "your power".; The offer can genuinely be started alone, so the new frame and the call to act point…
techniques.dilutes_when: The validation beat is skipped, so relocating the problem reads as blaming the reader for a real injury.; The outside cause really is the whole story, and the reader knows it, which makes the reframe feel like a dodge.; Control is granted by the seller rather than held by the reader, which leaves dependence in place under a freedom word.; The language stays abstract, all owning your journey and n…

techniques.name: Credentialed Consensus Break
techniques.lede: Cites credentialed experts breaking with the accepted view, or failing to agree among themselves, so a belief the reader treated as settled turns back into an open question.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy names people or bodies the reader already respects, doctors, studies, analysts, trade journals, then shows them contradicting the standard advice or splitting against one another. The claim is never that the reader was foolish. The claim is that the source of the settled answer has moved. A closed topic becomes an open one, which buys the writer room to lay out a different account of the problem before any product or offer is named.
techniques.why_it_works: Most readers skim past whatever they think they already know. That sense of knowing rests on a quiet assumption that the qualified people agree, so the fastest way to reopen the question is to show that they do not. A named credential carries the same weight the reader was already giving the old answer, which makes the contradiction hard to wave away. It also protects the reader's pride, since the error belonged to the experts and not to him, so attention opens instead of the usual guard going up.
techniques.lands_when: The expert is named and placed, with the credential stated in the copy rather than left to be assumed.; The disagreement lands on a specific belief the reader actually holds, not a vague swipe at the establishment.; The break is quoted or sourced, so the reader can picture where and when it was said.; A different account of the problem follows straight after, while the old belief is still loose.
techniques.dilutes_when: No real credential appears and the copy simply asserts that everyone else has it wrong.; The belief being broken is one the reader never held, so nothing is reopened.; The expert is wheeled in to approve the product rather than to contradict the accepted view.; The disagreement slides into a claim that the truth is being hidden, which asks for far more trust than a citation does.

techniques.name: Sell by Payment, Not Price
techniques.lede: The price never shrinks, but the number the buyer weighs against it does: quote the installment out loud and let the total fade, sometimes to a passing mention, sometimes out of the copy altogether.
techniques.what_it_does: This move splits the full price into a per-period payment and quotes that small figure loudest, while the real total recedes into the background: sometimes a passing mention, sometimes dropped from the copy entirely. The buyer's yes-or-no is decided against eight dollars a month or four easy payments, not against the whole number. It does not lower the price. It lowers the size of the figure the reader has to accept, so a large commitment reads as a small, familiar, recurring charge that slips under the threshold where a lump sum would trip an alarm.
techniques.why_it_works: People judge affordability against a mental threshold, and a small recurring figure clears it where the lump sum would not. A monthly or per-payment number also maps onto costs the buyer already tolerates, rent, a coffee, a phone bill, so the spend feels ordinary rather than exceptional. Splitting the total into installments buries the true magnitude behind arithmetic most readers never finish. And because the headline figure is genuinely small, the claim survives a second look: the payment really is that low, even when the price is not, so the reframe never feels like a lie.
techniques.lands_when: The item carries a big-ticket price that would stall the decision if it were shown first.; The installment figure maps onto an expense the buyer already accepts without thinking.; The full price stays visible somewhere, so the framing reads as a genuine option rather than a trick.; The payment is honestly low, so the small number withstands scrutiny.
techniques.dilutes_when: The per-payment figure is not much smaller than the total, so the split buys nothing.; Hidden interest or fees make the installments visibly add up to more, and trust collapses.; The buyer only needs the thing once, so a recurring charge reads as a trap rather than relief.; The whole pitch is payment terms with no reason to want the product in the first place.

techniques.name: The Anchor Price Reframe
techniques.lede: State a high reference price first, then reveal the real one, so the actual cost lands as a relief instead of a number to weigh.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy plants a large figure in the reader's mind before naming the price they will actually pay. That first number can be an old price, a retail tag, what a rival charges, what a professional would bill, or what the thing would cost built another way. Once that high anchor is set, the real price is read as the distance below it rather than on its own. A price that might feel steep in isolation feels like a saving, because the reader is now judging it against the bigger number sitting right beside it.
techniques.why_it_works: People have no fixed sense of what most things should cost, so they judge a price against whatever number is nearby. Drop a high figure first and it becomes the reference point every later number is measured from, a pull the mind cannot fully shake even when it knows the anchor was chosen for effect. The gap between the two numbers becomes the story, and the reader does the subtraction and feels the win. The actual price stops being a question of affordability and turns into evidence of a bargain already found.
techniques.lands_when: A genuinely higher reference is named first: a was-price, retail tag, rival's charge, or what a pro would bill; The gap between the anchor and the real price is wide enough to feel like a discovery, not a rounding error; The anchor is plausible, so the contrast reads as a real saving rather than an invented markdown; The real price follows close behind the anchor so the reader makes the compariso…
techniques.dilutes_when: The price appears alone with no higher number to be measured against; The anchor is a vague gesture at savings, a bare percentage with no dollar reference behind it; The high number is inflated past belief, so the contrast reads as a trick and the anchor loses its grip; A free-with-purchase or zero-price reveal takes over, making the giveaway the move rather than the price contrast

techniques.name: Competitor Contrast
techniques.lede: Set the product directly against a named rival or the old way, so the buyer judges it by the contrast rather than on its own.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy puts the product side by side with a competitor, a rival category, or the established way of doing things, then draws the line that makes the product the better pick. Sometimes it names the rival outright, sometimes it points at the ordinary version everyone already uses. Either way the reader is handed a reference point and a verdict at the same time. The claim stops being an abstract boast about the product and becomes a concrete choice between this and that.
techniques.why_it_works: People judge value by comparison, not in a vacuum. A price, a speed, or a feature means little until it sits next to something worse, and the mind reaches for the nearest reference point on its own. By supplying that reference point, the copy controls the frame the buyer uses to decide. Naming the rival also borrows its familiarity and steers the doubt onto it instead of the new product. Done with proof, the contrast reads as fair reporting rather than bragging, which lets the reader feel like they reached the verdict themselves.
techniques.lands_when: The rival or the old way is one the reader already knows and quietly measures against; A concrete point of difference carries the contrast: price, speed, ingredients, or a named result; The product genuinely wins on the axis chosen, so the comparison survives a skeptical check; The frame names the reference point the buyer was already using to judge the category
techniques.dilutes_when: No real competitor or old way is invoked, so the line collapses into a bare superlative; The move is really claiming a brand-new category, with no rival to contrast against; The contrast is against the buyer's own past, which is a before-and-after frame, not a rival; The chosen axis is vague or unprovable, so the comparison reads as an empty swipe

techniques.name: Categorical Reframe
techniques.lede: Tell the reader the thing in front of them belongs to a different category than they assumed, and every judgment they were about to make changes with it.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy takes the product, idea, or person and moves it out of the box the reader had already filed it under, then sets it down in a different, more favorable box. It does this in plain words: this is not a charity, it is a business model; this is not a bank; this is a fragrance house wearing the clothes of a grooming brand. By renaming the category, the writer resets the comparison set, the price the reader expects to pay, and the standard the thing gets judged against, all before a single feature is argued.
techniques.why_it_works: People judge by category first and details second. The moment something is filed as a vitamin, a toilet paper, an insurance company, the reader pulls up a ready-made set of expectations and prices and rivals. Naming a new category swaps that whole set out at once, so the old objections never get raised and the old price comparisons never get made. It also flatters the reader: accepting the new label means seeing past the obvious surface, which feels like insight rather than persuasion. The frame does the selling before the proof arrives.
techniques.lands_when: The new category is one the reader already respects, so the move trades up rather than into thin air.; The reassignment is stated outright, in words the reader can repeat, not merely implied by tone.; The old category carried a real liability (low price ceiling, tired rivals, distrust) that the swap escapes.; The rest of the copy then behaves like the new category, so the frame is paid off instea…
techniques.dilutes_when: The line only claims a better version of the same category, which is positioning, not a category swap.; The new label is invented from nothing and means nothing to the reader, so there is no respected box to enter.; The reframe is asserted but never supported, leaving a slogan the reader files back under the old category.; Several competing reframes stack in one breath, so no single new category…

techniques.name: Corporate Buyer Reframe
techniques.lede: The same pleasure purchase, handed to the company: bought for reasons a business can say out loud.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy keeps the desirable thing exactly as it is and changes who is buying it. Instead of speaking to a person weighing a treat, it speaks to an employer, a corporation, or whoever signs on the company's behalf, and attaches a business reason to the spend: reputation, new hires, closed deals, lower health costs, or simply a corporate price and an invoice. The pleasure usually stays in the sentence. What moves is the ledger the money is charged to.
techniques.why_it_works: A pleasure purchase is easy to argue with while one person is paying for it. Move the decision onto an organization and the argument changes shape, because a company is expected to spend on its image, its people, and its sales, so the same money reads as ordinary business rather than self-indulgence. The reader is handed a reason they can repeat out loud to a partner, a board, or an accountant. The enjoyment is usually left in view; it just stops being the thing that has to be defended.
techniques.lands_when: The item is genuinely enjoyable, and a buyer would feel silly justifying it on personal taste alone.; The organization has a real interest the purchase touches: hiring, client relationships, reputation, or a cost it already carries.; The reader can actually spend company money, and the copy addresses them in that role rather than as a private shopper.; The business reason is plain enough to survi…
techniques.dilutes_when: The product was already a business purchase, so there is no personal spend left to relocate.; The business reason stays vague, so the reader has nothing concrete to repeat to anyone holding the money.; The pleasure is scrubbed out entirely, leaving a flat equipment pitch with nothing left to want.; The company benefit is obviously invented, and the reader sees a personal treat wearing a business…

techniques.name: The Upstream Move
techniques.lede: The Upstream Move sends the reader's effort one step back in the chain, off the symptom they have been fighting and onto the thing that keeps producing it.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy names the thing the reader is currently working on, the ads, the diet, the pain, the stock picks, and demotes it. Then it points one step earlier in the chain to whatever produces that thing, and puts the effort there instead. The usual shapes are a not-this-but-that sentence, an effects versus causes contrast, or an ordering rule saying settle the earlier question before touching the later one. The reader is never told to try harder, only to move where they push.
techniques.why_it_works: Failed effort gets an explanation that costs the reader nothing in self respect: they were working, just in the wrong place. That keeps the past honest while making the future look cheap, because a small correction early is presented as worth more than any amount of grinding late. It also opens a gap in knowledge. The reader knows the downstream job well and the upstream one hardly at all, so whoever names the earlier cause becomes the obvious person to sell the fix for it.
techniques.lands_when: The reader has already tried the obvious fix and watched it fail to hold.; The link between the two points is short enough to picture in one sentence.; The upstream thing is something the reader can actually reach and change.; The copy names what the reader is doing now before it names what to do instead.
techniques.dilutes_when: The cause named is so far back that nothing the reader does can touch it.; The relocation is asserted as a slogan with no chain shown between cause and result.; The symptom is still urgent and painful, so waving it aside reads as being dismissed.; Every seller in the category relocates to the same cause, which turns an insight into a formula.

techniques.name: Workforce Reframe
techniques.lede: Workforce Reframe sells a machine as staff you take on rather than equipment you buy, so the buyer weighs it against a wage instead of a purchase price.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy swaps the category word. In place of machine, appliance, tool or licence, the product gets a staffing word: servant, hand, clerk, operator, worker, hire, teammate, agent. Some versions say the old category out loud and refuse it, others skip straight to the new one. Duties usually follow in the same breath, the jobs a person on payroll or in service would own. The strongest versions put a wage on the other side of the comparison: coal against a fireman's hours, fuel against feed and a driver, a machine's running cost against what a laundress or a clerk is paid. When that arithmetic appears, the reader is no longer comparing products at all.
techniques.why_it_works: Buyers keep separate mental budgets. Equipment competes on a small line against other equipment, while labour sits on a much larger one, so moving the product into the staffing column changes the number it is compared with and makes almost any price look modest. Staffing words also carry ownership. A worker is answerable for a job finished, a tool is only responsible for making a job easier, so the frame quietly promises outcomes rather than features. Naming the old category and refusing it forces the reader to re-file the product before pricing it. The frame reaches hardest where the human it replaces is scarce, expensive, or hard to keep.
techniques.lands_when: The product genuinely owns a whole job end to end, so the staffing word survives the first demo; The buyer already carries that job on payroll and the wage is the number in their head; Concrete duties travel with the staffing word, so the claim has visible work attached to it; The seller can hold the frame past the headline, in how it is priced, set up, and supported
techniques.dilutes_when: The product only helps a person who still does the job, so calling it a worker overpromises; The staffing word arrives bare, with no duties behind it, and reads as a slogan; Every seller in the category has adopted the same word, so it no longer sorts anything; The wage comparison invites a like-for-like audit on judgment and accountability that the product cannot pass; The machine is merely call…

techniques.name: Category-Analogy Reframe
techniques.lede: A one-line analogy that defines a product by borrowing a familiar category from another market, handing the reader its whole mental model in a single phrase.
techniques.what_it_does: It pins an unfamiliar or hard-to-place product to a category the reader already understands, in a single phrase. By naming that known category, the copy borrows its entire mental model at once: the commitment, the frequency of use, the rough price shape, the feel, the status. All of it transfers to the product without a word of explanation. The reader does the work, filling in the meaning from what they already know about the category being borrowed.
techniques.why_it_works: The mind files new things by matching them to patterns it already holds. Naming a familiar category hands the reader a ready-made frame, so they grasp what the product is, how often they would use it, roughly what it costs, and why it should matter, almost instantly. The borrowed category's feelings and status ride along with it. And because the reader supplies the detail from their own memory, the positioning feels obvious rather than claimed, which quietly lowers the urge to argue.
techniques.lands_when: The borrowed category is one the audience knows cold, so the mapping needs no footnote.; The transferred model is accurate on the traits that matter: price shape, frequency, feel, or status.; The product is new or hard to categorize, and the analogy gives it an instant shelf to sit on.; One clean line carries it, and the reader gets the whole idea before deciding whether to agree.
techniques.dilutes_when: The borrowed category is obscure, or means different things to different readers.; The analogy flatters on a trait the product cannot deliver, so the mapping breaks on contact.; It is stacked with three more analogies, so no single mental model ever takes hold.; The reader already knows the category well, and the comparison shrinks the product to a mere copy.

techniques.name: Positioning Reframe
techniques.lede: Positioning Reframe redraws the map a buyer uses to place a brand, so the familiar category leaders end up on the wrong side of the line.
techniques.what_it_does: It takes the frame a shopper already carries into a category and quietly redraws it. Instead of competing on the accepted terms, the copy renames what the brand is, what its choice means, or where it sits against the familiar players. A rental counter becomes a marketplace, a store closure becomes a stand, a routine product becomes a movement. The reader keeps the comparison but changes which end looks modern, honest, or smart, and the incumbent is left defending the older definition of the category.
techniques.why_it_works: People judge a product by the category slot they file it in, and that slot carries a default set of rivals and rules. Change the slot and every comparison changes with it, so the brand no longer has to win the old contest on the old terms. A reframe also flatters the reader, because accepting the new frame makes them feel a step ahead of everyone still shopping the tired way. Since it argues about meaning rather than features, it is hard to answer with a spec sheet, and it sticks as a story the buyer retells.
techniques.lands_when: The copy names the old category or rival on purpose, then plants the brand outside it.; A single clean line carries the reframe, so the reader adopts it before weighing features.; The new frame flatters the reader for seeing past the familiar way to shop.; The brand can actually deliver on the new definition it claims to occupy.
techniques.dilutes_when: The line only lists benefits, so there is no old frame being replaced.; It attacks a rival but leaves the brand's own position undefined.; It invents a category with no rival present, which reads as jargon rather than a reframe.; The claimed new position stays vague, so the reader cannot picture the old one it beats.

techniques.name: Big Idea Frame
techniques.lede: Open with a big governing story or image so every fact that follows is read through it.
techniques.what_it_does: Before any claim, proof, or offer arrives, the copy installs a large interpretive frame: a parable, an allegory, a historical analogy, or a self-announced story. That frame becomes the lens. Once the reader accepts it, the details that follow are no longer judged on their own; they are slotted into the meaning the frame already supplied. The argument feels less like a pitch and more like the natural next chapter of a story the reader has already started believing.
techniques.why_it_works: People reach for a frame to make sense of new information, and they use whichever one is handed to them first. By setting the frame ahead of the claims, the copy decides in advance what the facts will mean, so the reader does the persuading from the inside. A story also lowers the guard that a direct argument raises: we resist being sold, but we lean into being told a story. By the time the real claim lands, it reads as confirmation of something the reader already feels, not as a request to be weighed.
techniques.lands_when: The frame is set before the facts, not bolted on after, so it can color how everything reads.; The governing image is large enough to absorb the whole pitch, not a one-line flourish.; The reader is pulled into the story before they notice a product is involved.; The eventual claim clicks into the frame as its natural payoff rather than a hard turn.
techniques.dilutes_when: The frame arrives after the claims, so it decorates rather than governs.; The metaphor is vivid but local, coloring one line instead of the whole argument.; The story is so long or self-pleased that the actual point never lands.; The frame and the claim do not connect, leaving the reader with a tale and a non-sequitur.

techniques.name: Beyond-Reach List
techniques.lede: A list of concrete places and moments the product covers that the usual option can't, so the reader counts their own week instead of weighing a claim.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy names specific situations, on the train, in a hotel room, in bright sunlight, in a deep crevice, and puts the product in each one where the usual choice fails, is left behind, or can't reach. The old option is named or clearly implied: the tablet that glares, the brush that can't get into corners, the desktop that stays at the office, the vacuum confined to the floor. The situations do the comparing, so the copy rarely needs a rival brand or a general superiority claim. What it sells is reach: the list of places the reader now gets to bring the thing.
techniques.why_it_works: A general claim invites a general answer. A named place invites a memory. When copy says 'in your hotel room' or 'in bright sunlight', the reader tests it against a real week, and the test tends to settle the point before the product is even weighed. Because the reader supplies that evidence, the case reads as observation rather than boast. Each place also carries its own small comparison, since the reader knows what the usual option does there, so the list does competitive work without an attack on anyone.
techniques.lands_when: The places are ones the reader visits in an ordinary week, not exotic edge cases.; Each place quietly names what the usual option cannot do there.; The list stays short enough to be checked, three to six situations, then stops.; The product is shown doing the same job in the new place, not a lesser version of it.
techniques.dilutes_when: The situations are generic, 'anywhere, anytime', so nothing maps onto a real place.; The list slides into features with no place attached to them.; No old option is named or implied, so the list reads as versatility rather than reach.; A named situation is one the product does not actually serve, which hands the reader an objection.

techniques.name: Nostalgia Appeal
techniques.lede: Nostalgia Appeal reaches into a specific memory from the audience's own past and lets its warmth carry over onto the product, sometimes framing the present as a falling-off from that earlier time.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy summons a specific past: a childhood breakfast, a first thrill, a country that felt whole, a body that worked without complaint. Often it measures the present against that memory and finds it thinner, faker, or harder; other times the memory plays on its own, carrying no complaint about now. Into that memory steps the offer, presented not as something new but as a way back: the taste you remember, the feeling you lost, the standard everyone else abandoned. Buying stops being a purchase and becomes an act of return.
techniques.why_it_works: Memory flatters the past. People recall old summers, old prices, and younger versions of themselves with the rough edges sanded off, so the invoked era arrives pre-approved. Longing for it registers as loss, and people work harder to recover what they once had than to gain something new. The remembered scene also carries identity: it tells the reader this is who you really are, and the product borrows that warmth. A claim wrapped inside the customer's own memory meets far less resistance than a claim about the product.
techniques.lands_when: The audience genuinely shares the invoked memory, a common childhood staple or an era they lived through.; The product can plausibly restore something the buyer once had: a taste, a feeling, a capability, a standard.; Concrete sensory detail places the reader inside the remembered scene instead of telling them it was good.; The present-day gap is real and already felt, so the contrast reads as re…
techniques.dilutes_when: The audience is too young or too varied to have lived the memory being invoked.; The past is praised in vague terms, the good old days, with no specific scene to re-enter.; The product cannot credibly deliver the return, so the promise reads as sentiment stapled onto a pitch.; The copy slides into grievance about the present, souring the warm feeling the move depends on.

techniques.name: Category of One Reframe
techniques.lede: Draw the category so narrowly that the product is the only thing in it, and there is nothing left to compare it against.
techniques.what_it_does: This move draws the boundary of a category so tightly that only the offer fits inside it. Instead of claiming to be the best option, it claims to be the sole option, using language like the only, no other, one of a kind, or in a class by itself. The reader is handed a set with a single member, so the usual work of weighing rivals has nothing to act on. Comparison shopping quietly disappears, because there is no second thing to line the offer up against.
techniques.why_it_works: People decide by comparing, and a category with one member removes the thing they would compare against. With no visible substitute, price checks and feature grids lose their footing, and the offer starts to feel less like a purchase and more like the only way to get a specific result. The claim also flatters the buyer's judgment, since choosing the singular thing feels smarter than picking from a crowd. Framed this way, the product reads as a reference point rather than a contestant, which is exactly where premium and high-ticket positioning wants to sit.
techniques.lands_when: The narrowed category is built around a real, nameable difference the reader can point to, not a vague boast.; The wording forecloses comparison outright ('the only,' 'no other'), rather than ranking the offer above peers.; The single distinguishing feature actually matters to the buyer's decision.; Surrounding copy backs the sole-member claim with a mechanism, credential, or proof so it reads as…
techniques.dilutes_when: The uniqueness rests on a trivial or invented distinction the reader sees straight through.; The claim slides into a superlative ('best,' 'most'), which readmits the comparison it was meant to close.; Rivals plainly offer the same thing, so 'only' reads as false and burns trust.; The category is drawn so narrowly that it sounds like word games instead of a real difference.

techniques.name: Selfless Video Reason
techniques.lede: A stated reason the offer or the video exists that points at something other than money.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy stops to explain why this thing was made, and the explanation lands somewhere other than profit. The shapes vary: a sacrifice the seller made, effort spent long before the reader arrived, a charitable purpose the money serves, a mission the sender says the offer advances, or a flat statement that the seller does not need the income. It usually arrives in the first person as a short story, and sometimes as an account of what a company decided to do.
techniques.why_it_works: A reader who knows a sale is coming reads every claim as self-interested. Naming a motive other than money gives the copy a purpose the reader cannot file under greed, and it answers a question the reader was already forming. Effort and sacrifice carry extra weight, since a night without sleep or a year of persuading someone is a cost the seller paid before any sale existed. A stated purpose also tells the reader what the transaction means, which is harder to argue with than a claim about the product.
techniques.lands_when: The reason is specific enough to picture: a named person, a named stretch of time, a named thing the seller gave up.; It comes early, before the price and before the pitch, while the reader is still deciding what this is.; The cost to the seller is stated plainly rather than implied by tone.; The motive named matches what the rest of the copy actually does.

techniques.name: Majority Is Wrong Reframe
techniques.lede: Majority Is Wrong Reframe takes the thing everyone believes or the way the whole crowd is reacting and turns that consensus itself into the reader's opening.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy points at something the audience takes for granted: a belief everyone shares, an industry habit, or the way the crowd is reacting to a piece of news. Then it flips the sign. The fact that most people think this thing, or do this thing, becomes the reason it is wrong, and the reason a reader who breaks from the pack comes out ahead. The herd's reaction stops being a fact to accept and becomes the opening to exploit.
techniques.why_it_works: People want to feel like the one who sees what others miss, and this move hands them that role for free. Consensus normally feels safe, so naming it out loud and then calling it the mistake creates a small jolt that makes the reader lean in. It also does quiet flattery: if the crowd is wrong, the reader who agrees with the writer is among the smart minority. And by tying the crowd's error to a concrete opening, it turns a plain observation into a reason to act now rather than later.
techniques.lands_when: The consensus it names is one the reader genuinely recognizes as widespread, not a strawman built to knock down.; The flip points to a concrete opening or advantage, not merely the claim that everyone else is foolish.; The counter-position is one the reader can actually take, so the arbitrage feels available to them.; The tone stays calmly confident, as if stating a known edge, rather than contra…
techniques.dilutes_when: The majority it attacks is vague or invented, so the reframe fights no belief the reader actually holds.; It stops at debunking and never shows the opportunity the crowd's error is supposed to create.; The contrarian claim rests on nothing, so it reads as posture instead of a real insight.; The reader is already in the flattered minority, so there is no live consensus left to flip.

techniques.name: Hidden-in-Plain-Sight Frame
techniques.lede: It points at something already public and shows the reader the important thing was sitting inside it the whole time, unnoticed.
techniques.what_it_does: The writer takes a document, form, product fact, or everyday object that anyone could have looked at, then pulls out a consequential detail buried inside it. The persuasive charge is not that the information was locked away or censored. It is that the item was open, checkable, and in front of the reader, who walked right past it. The move casts the writer as the one person who finally read closely, and it makes the claim feel verifiable because the source is real and out in the open.
techniques.why_it_works: Because the item is public, a reader cannot easily wave the claim off as invention. It borrows the authority of a real source anyone could inspect. The gap between available and noticed produces a small jolt of self-reproach that reads as insight, not sales talk. It also sidesteps the guard people raise against cover-up stories, since nothing was suppressed, only overlooked. And it hands the reader a flattering new role: from this moment on they are one of the few who see what was always sitting there.

techniques.dilutes_when: The public source is vague or unnamed, leaving nothing the reader could actually check.; The copy slides into suppression or cover-up language, which swaps this frame for a harder claim to believe.; The buried detail is trivial, so the you-missed-this jolt never fires.; So many hidden documents are stacked up that none of them feels checkable anymore.

techniques.name: Access Democratization Frame
techniques.lede: It recasts buying the product as joining a club that used to keep ordinary people out.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy names a domain that has long been walled off, reserved for the rich, for insiders, for credentialed professionals, and then positions the product as the thing that knocks the wall down. The buyer is no longer a customer weighing a purchase; they are a person finally let through a door that money or status used to guard. The frame trades on a felt unfairness, points at the gate, and hands the reader the key, turning a transaction into a small act of leveling.
techniques.why_it_works: It borrows the energy of a grievance most people already carry: the sense that the good stuff is rigged for someone else. By naming the gatekept class out loud, the copy validates that resentment, then resolves it in the reader's favor, which feels like justice rather than salesmanship. The product inherits the prestige of the elite world it claims to open, while the buyer gets to feel both savvy and righteous for crossing the line. Belonging and fairness do the persuading, so price and features recede behind a story about who finally gets in.
techniques.lands_when: The copy names a specific gatekept group the reader resents being outside of, the wealthy, the insiders, the big players; The barrier being removed is concrete and believable, a price floor, a credential, a paywall, an invite-only door; The reader genuinely sits on the excluded side, so the open door reads as their win; The product is the plausible agent of the opening, not just a beneficiary of…
techniques.dilutes_when: No elite or insider class is named, so the line is generic affordability with no one to be let in past; The brand still signals exclusivity elsewhere, making the open-door claim ring hollow; The promise is vague uplift ('elevate your life') with no gate and no excluded group; The reader was never shut out of the domain, so there is no wall to tear down and the frame falls flat

techniques.name: Autonomy Frame
techniques.lede: Position the product as the thing that hands control back to a person the world keeps stripping it from.
techniques.what_it_does: Autonomy Frame casts the buyer as the rightful owner of a decision, a schedule, a body, or a set of data, and casts the product as the means of taking that control back. The copy speaks in the second person and in verbs of choice: you decide, you set, you keep, the choice is yours. It names a domain the reader assumed was fixed or governed by someone else, then returns the steering wheel. The promise is not a feature or a saving but restored self-direction.
techniques.why_it_works: People resist being told what to do and prize the feeling of having chosen freely, so copy that returns a decision to the reader lowers resistance and raises the value they place on the offer. Naming the control explicitly flatters the reader as competent and trustworthy rather than managed. It also reframes the purchase as an act of self-respect, which makes saying yes feel like an assertion of agency instead of a concession. The move works hardest where buyers feel boxed in by contracts, gatekeepers, defaults, or rigid systems.

techniques.dilutes_when: The control language is mood or identity dressing with no decision actually handed over; Every product claims it, so the frame reads as a category cliche rather than a real difference; The promised control is contradicted by fine print, lock-in, or hidden defaults; It is stacked under a louder move (price, social proof, asset ownership) that actually carries the copy

techniques.name: Make Invisible Measurable
techniques.lede: This technique takes something a reader could always feel but never see, and turns it into a named number they can watch and move.
techniques.what_it_does: It converts an abstract, unquantified dimension of life, such as stress, aging, sleep quality, focus, or where the money goes, into a named metric: a score, a chart, a tracked reading. Naming and numbering the invisible thing makes it feel real. Once it is real, it can be compared over time, judged against a baseline, and improved. The product presents itself as the instrument, the only lens through which this hidden dimension becomes visible at all.
techniques.why_it_works: People discount what they cannot see. A number gives an abstraction edges: a starting point, a direction, a better and a worse. Measurement also implies control; if something can be scored, it can be managed, so a vague background worry becomes a concrete task with a visible payoff. The move converts anxiety into agency. It also builds a habit loop, because once a score exists the reader wants to check it, and the metric belongs to the product, so improving the number keeps the reader inside it.
techniques.lands_when: The dimension genuinely matters to the reader but has stayed vague and unnamed, like energy, stress, aging, or cash flow.; The metric is graspable at a glance: one name, one scale, an obvious better and worse.; The reader can plausibly move the number through actions the product helps them take.; The measurement promises to reveal something the reader could not have sensed on their own.
techniques.dilutes_when: The thing was already familiar and measurable, so the new metric adds a label rather than new sight.; Too many scores arrive at once and the reader cannot tell which number is the point.; The metric comes with no clear action attached, so the number sits there as decoration.; The reader suspects the score is arbitrary and the copy cannot show what it is built from.

techniques.name: Unexpected Mechanism Reveal
techniques.lede: The product refuses the one method its whole category is assumed to use, and names a different kind of method in its place.
techniques.what_it_does: A buyer arrives already holding a mechanism in mind, the method every product in the category is assumed to run on. The copy names that method and refuses it, then puts a different kind of method where it was. The refusal is about kind, not degree: the product is not a stronger version of the usual thing, it is a different sort of thing. Most versions run in two beats, a denial and a substitute, then a short account of how the substitute does the job the old method was supposed to do.
techniques.why_it_works: Inside a category, buyers rank on one shared axis, so every claim collapses into a claim of being better. Denying the shared method lifts the product off that axis, and there is suddenly nothing obvious to rank it against. The denial also gives the reader a clean account of past failure that costs them nothing: none of it worked because all of it used the same wrong method. And a flat contradiction of what the reader believed a second ago opens a gap only the next sentence can close, so they keep reading to find out what replaces it.
techniques.lands_when: The category really does share one obvious method a reader can name without help.; The substitute is named plainly and can be explained in a sentence or two.; The reader has already tried the standard method and it failed them.; The denial comes early, before the reader files the product on the usual shelf.
techniques.dilutes_when: The claimed difference is only a better version of the same method, so the denial reads as bluster.; The copy refuses the standard method but never names what takes its place.; The substitute falls apart the moment a reader asks how it actually works.; The reader has no picture of the category yet, so there is nothing to turn over.

techniques.name: The Governing Metaphor
techniques.lede: One concrete image takes over the whole message, and every claim is made in its terms.
techniques.what_it_does: This move picks a single vivid picture, a machine, a creature, a body, a building, and lets it govern the entire piece. The product, the problem, and the proof all get described in that picture's language. Instead of arguing point by point, the copy asks the reader to accept one image, then everything that follows feels like a natural consequence of it. The image carries the logic, so the reader reasons the writer's way without being told to.
techniques.why_it_works: A good image gives scattered facts a single shape the mind can hold. Once a reader accepts that a business is a machine or a threat is a bear, the conclusions the writer wants feel like simple common sense rather than a sales pitch, because they follow from a picture the reader has already agreed to. The image also does emotional work the plain claim cannot: it makes an abstract risk feel physical and a dull benefit feel concrete. One frame, repeated, is easier to remember and harder to argue with than a list.
techniques.lands_when: The image maps cleanly onto the real subject, so each part of the picture stands for a real part of the offer or problem; The copy keeps reasoning inside the image rather than dropping it after the headline; The picture is concrete and familiar enough that the reader pictures it instantly; The chosen image carries the exact feeling the argument needs, danger, comfort, growth, decay
techniques.dilutes_when: The image is decorative, a single pretty phrase that never organizes anything around it; Two or three unrelated images compete, so no single frame governs; The picture is so abstract or generic that it adds no concrete logic the plain claim lacked; The mapping breaks down on inspection, and the reader notices the parts do not actually correspond

techniques.name: Value Framing
techniques.lede: Value Framing sets the price beside what the buyer gets for it, so the spend stops looking like a cost and starts looking like a bargain.
techniques.what_it_does: It reframes a price against the value it delivers instead of letting the number stand alone. The copy breaks the cost into a tiny daily or per-use figure, lines it up against a familiar everyday expense, totals up what the buyer would otherwise spend or save, or shows how much value rides on a small outlay. The dollar figure does not change. What changes is the yardstick the reader measures it against, so the same price feels small, fair, or obviously worth it.
techniques.why_it_works: People do not judge a price in isolation. They judge it against a reference point, and whoever supplies that reference point controls how the number feels. A yearly fee divided into pennies a day, or a price set next to a restaurant dinner, shrinks the perceived sacrifice without touching the actual sum. Tying the spend to the value it unlocks also shifts attention from what leaves the wallet to what comes back. The buyer stops asking whether they can afford it and starts asking whether they can afford to pass it up.
techniques.lands_when: The price is named and set explicitly beside the value, savings, or a concrete reference cost; The reference point is one the reader already understands, like a daily coffee or a single client; The math is easy to follow in one read, so the bargain registers without effort; The value claimed is believable for the category, so the comparison does not feel like a stretch
techniques.dilutes_when: The copy quotes a price or strikethrough discount but never weighs it against any value; It promises a return multiple where the real pull is the gain, not the smallness of the spend; The comparison value is wildly inflated, so the reader distrusts the whole frame; It leans on emotional payoff or features alone with no cost actually placed in the balance

techniques.name: Body as Oracle Frame
techniques.lede: Copy that treats the body as something already speaking, and casts the product as the thing that lets its owner finally hear it.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy grants the body a voice, or signals, or needs it is already expressing, then puts the product in the smaller role of translator, listener, or tuner. A reading stops being a verdict handed down about the reader and becomes a report from inside the reader. The shape varies. Some versions state it flatly as a promise, some set listening against scorekeeping and benchmarks, and some take a number and render it as a plain statement of what the body is going through and what it seems to want.
techniques.why_it_works: Being measured invites resistance, because a measurement implies an outside judge holding standards the reader never agreed to. Recasting the same data as the body's own speech removes the judge. The reader is not failing a test, they are hearing themselves, and pushing back on the reading starts to feel like pushing back on their own body. The frame also leans on something people already half believe, that the body knows things before the mind puts them into words. The product gains trust by claiming less: it carries a message rather than issuing one.

techniques.name: Commerce Not Charity Reframe
techniques.lede: The copy refuses the charity label for the reader's money and files the same act under commerce instead: a purchase, an investment, or a business that has to pay its own way.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy names the category the reader is about to reach for, charity, donation, handout, gift, and rules it out, then supplies a commercial category in its place: a business model, an investment, a purchase, a loan. Often the substitution is walked through step by step, showing where the money goes and what comes back. The reader's act keeps its moral payoff but changes its accounting, moving from money given away to money put to work.
techniques.why_it_works: Giving is filed in a mental account marked loss, which raises two familiar defenses: doubt about where the money lands, and the quiet resentment of being asked to sacrifice. Commerce is filed differently. A purchase carries an expectation of value returned, an investment carries a return, and a business is expected to sustain itself rather than come back asking. Swapping the label swaps the questions the reader asks. It also protects standing: the reader becomes a customer or an investor with judgment, not a soft touch being worked.
techniques.lands_when: The money genuinely moves through a trade, a loan, or a sale, and the copy can trace each step.; The reader's main resistance is the feeling that giving is a bottomless drain with nothing to show for it.; The buyer receives something real of their own, so the commercial label is literally true.; The new category arrives with figures the brand will show: costs, prices, repayment, results per dolla…
techniques.dilutes_when: The word business is claimed while the money still flows exactly like a donation.; The charity label is denied and no replacement is offered, leaving the reader unsure what they just did.; The appeal depends on pity for its urgency, so removing the sacrifice removes the reason to act now.; The commercial language runs long enough that the people being helped turn into line items.

techniques.name: Heritage as Resale Premium Warrant
techniques.lede: A brand makes age, whether the product's own wear or the maker's history, the reason the price holds, so the piece reads as a value that lasts rather than one that depreciates.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy takes what could count against the product, wear on the unit itself or simply the years since the brand or its craft tradition began, and names it as the source of value. Age is not discounted, it is charged for. The claim runs forward, saying the thing will still be worth having in twenty years, or backward, saying the worn unit in front of you is better than a new one. Either way the price is warranted by time rather than by newness.
techniques.why_it_works: Most categories train buyers to read wear as loss, so a price that survives use feels like proof of build quality instead of a claim about it. The frame also turns a purchase into a holding: if the thing keeps its worth, the money is parked rather than spent, which quiets the part of the buyer that resists paying more. And a used unit carrying a premium implies other people wanted it, so the second-hand market does the vouching. Time becomes evidence a new competitor cannot buy.
techniques.lands_when: The category has a visible second-hand market whose prices a reader can go and check.; The material really does change with use in a way a buyer can name, such as leather, denim, cast iron, or wood.; The price is high enough that the buyer is already hunting for a reason to justify it.; The maker has been around long enough that old units are still in circulation and still wanted.

techniques.name: Outcome-Without-Method Paradox
techniques.lede: Promise the result while striking out the very method everyone assumes is required to get it.
techniques.what_it_does: This move pairs a wanted outcome with the negation of its own canonical method. It names the result, then cancels the tool, ingredient, labor, or process the reader takes for granted as the price of that result. The salon look arrives without the salon; the broadcast quality without the studio; the cool sleep from the foam that is supposed to run hot. The copy stages a small contradiction and resolves it in the product's favor, so the reader feels the relief of skipping a step they had already braced for.
techniques.why_it_works: Buyers carry an unspoken script for how a result gets made, and most of that script is dread: the cost, the time, the discomfort, the skill. By naming the outcome and deleting its assumed method in one stroke, the line short-circuits that dread before it can become an objection. The paradox also reads as proof of a better way: if the usual labor is no longer needed, something genuinely new must be doing the work. Curiosity does the rest, because the reader now wants to know how the result survives without its cause.
techniques.lands_when: The negated thing is the method readers actually assume is required, not a generic hassle; The outcome named is specific and desirable enough that skipping its method feels like a real win; A believable reason or mechanism stands behind the missing method, so the paradox does not read as a lie; The contrast is tight, with result and method-negation close together in one beat
techniques.dilutes_when: The 'without' only removes a vague pain or objection, collapsing into an ordinary benefit line; No canonical method is named, so there is no paradox to resolve; The promise stacks so many negations that none reads as the assumed cost being cancelled; The claim outruns belief, and the missing method reads as a corner cut rather than a smarter path

techniques.name: The Trivial Equivalent
techniques.lede: The price is set beside something the reader already buys without thinking, so the number stops reading as a decision and starts reading as loose change.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy names its price, then names something the reader buys in a normal week for about the same money: a coffee, a lunch, a small treat. The two amounts are held side by side so the reader notices they match. The comparison object is picked for being habitual and unexamined, not simply for being cheap. Often the price is first cut down to a daily or weekly figure, so that a single routine purchase is large enough to cover it, and only then is the everyday item placed next to it.
techniques.why_it_works: People do not judge a price on its own. They judge it against whatever it is being compared to, and the seller chooses the comparison. A purchase the reader already makes without thinking carries a settled verdict, worth it, no decision needed, and the price borrows that verdict when the two are lined up. The question quietly changes from whether the reader can afford the thing to whether it beats a cup of coffee, and that second question is far easier to answer yes to.
techniques.lands_when: The comparison names a purchase this particular reader actually makes, not a generic one.; The two amounts are close enough that the reader does not have to stretch to see the match.; The payoff on offer is large next to the everyday item, so the trade looks lopsided in the reader's favor.; The price is genuinely small, or has already been cut to a daily figure that one habit could cover.
techniques.dilutes_when: The everyday item costs a fraction of the real price, so the match feels like sleight of hand.; The reader does not buy the named item, and the line quietly reveals that the seller does not know them.; The same worn comparison turns up in every offer in the category, so it reads as filler rather than argument.; The purchase is large or carefully considered, where shrinking it to pocket change ins…

techniques.name: The Category Creation
techniques.lede: Position the offering as a brand-new kind of thing rather than a better version of an existing one, so buyers have nothing to compare it against.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy refuses the obvious shelf the product would sit on and names a new one instead. Instead of arguing the thing is faster, cheaper, or better than its rivals, it declares the thing is a different kind of thing entirely: a first of its kind, a new class, a third option, a coined category with its own name. Once the reader accepts the new label, the old rivals stop being rivals, because they belong to a category the product has stepped out of.
techniques.why_it_works: Comparison is how buyers protect themselves, and it needs at least two members of one category. A product that claims to be the only member of a new category removes the yardstick: there is no cheaper alternative, no established leader, no track record to lose to. The reader cannot ask 'better than what' because nothing else is in the box. Naming the category also hands the reader a ready-made way to think and talk about the thing, and the brand that supplies the name tends to own the meaning. The product becomes the definition, not a contestant.
techniques.lands_when: The new category is named in plain words a reader can repeat, not just implied by tone.; The old category it steps away from is recognizable, so the reader feels the gap being opened.; The product can actually deliver something the old category cannot, so the new label survives a second look.; The brand is early or credible enough to be believed as the thing's definition rather than a latecomer r…
techniques.dilutes_when: The line only claims to be best or first within the existing category, which is a superiority claim, not a new category.; The new label is empty dressing over an ordinary product, so the reader reattaches the old comparison at once.; The copy names a category so broad or vague that it carries no meaning and triggers no recognition.; Several competitors crowd the same coined category, collapsing i…

techniques.name: Your-Real-Number Reveal
techniques.lede: Tells the reader that the number they have been going by is not their real number, then puts a different measure of the same thing in its place.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy takes a figure the reader already lives by, most often their age, and says it is the wrong figure. In its place it puts another measure of the same thing: a branded score, a plain contrast between the calendar and the body, or a pair of opposing measures pulling in different directions. The distance between the old figure and the new one becomes the reader's real position. Some versions stop at naming that distance; others point at what moves it.
techniques.why_it_works: A number the reader has accepted for years feels settled. Naming a second measure of the same thing unsettles it without contradicting anything the reader believes, since both numbers can be true at once. The gap that opens is about the reader personally rather than about a product, so it earns attention before any claim is made. It also turns a vague worry into something with a direction and a size, which makes the worry feel like a thing that can be worked on instead of just carried.
techniques.lands_when: The reader already carries a default number for the thing being measured, so the substitute has something to push against.; The new measure comes with a plain meaning attached, so the reader knows which direction counts as better.; The gap is presented as movable rather than as a fixed verdict on the reader.; The measure connects to something in the reader's ordinary week, so it reads as their nu…
techniques.dilutes_when: The new measure arrives with no stated meaning, so a figure lands with nothing riding on it.; The old number was never the reader's reference point, so there is no gap for them to feel.; Several invented measures stack up at once and the reader cannot hold on to any of them.; The gap reads as a permanent score, which invites the reader to look away instead of closer.

techniques.name: Earned Entitlement Reframe
techniques.lede: Recast the offer not as buying something new but as claiming something the reader has already earned and is now being denied.
techniques.what_it_does: This move flips the frame on a purchase or sign-up. Instead of asking the reader to spend, it tells them they already own, earned, or deserve the thing, and that inaction, paperwork, or a middleman is the only reason they do not have it yet. The product becomes the path to reclaiming what is rightfully theirs. The decision shifts from 'should I buy this?' to 'why have I not collected what I am owed?' Refusing now feels like leaving your own money on the table.
techniques.why_it_works: People hate losing what is theirs far more than they enjoy gaining something new. By naming the benefit as already earned, the copy converts a discretionary purchase into the recovery of a loss, which carries more urgency and less price resistance. It also flatters the reader's sense of merit: you served, you worked, you drove safely, so this is your due. The seller stops being a vendor asking for money and becomes an ally helping you claim it back, which lowers suspicion and reframes the price as a small cost to unlock a larger sum that is rightfully yours.
techniques.lands_when: The reader plausibly has a real claim behind the copy: earned wages, filed benefits, an overpayment, a right written into law.; The withholding party can be named or clearly pointed at, so the blame lands somewhere specific instead of on bad luck.; The offer genuinely helps retrieve the thing, and the copy can say how the money or the rating actually comes back.; The payoff is concrete enough to…
techniques.dilutes_when: Nothing was ever owed, so the entitlement is invented and the reader can feel the stretch.; An ordinary purchase is dressed as a recovery, with no claim, filing, or enforcement standing behind it.; The institution is left so vague that nobody is blamed and nothing reads as withheld.; The retrieval promise outruns what the seller can do, leaving the reader to work the claim alone anyway.

techniques.name: Wrong Fear, Real Danger
techniques.lede: Take the cause the reader already blames off the table, then point at a different one as the thing that actually decides the outcome.
techniques.what_it_does: The copy names the explanation a reader is already carrying and denies it, then puts another cause in its place. What gets denied can be a single suspect or a short run of them, and it can be the reader's own effort or an assumption about where a decision really gets made. The replacement is sometimes stated plainly and sometimes held back as something hidden the reader has not heard of yet, and the shortest versions stop at the denial and leave the replacement for later.
techniques.why_it_works: A reader who has already settled on why something happens is not neutral, and the denial interrupts that settled account before a new one arrives. Because the rejected cause is often the thing the reader has already tried, taking it away can land as relief rather than argument, since the effort was aimed at the wrong target. The new cause then arrives with a job waiting for it, and whatever can answer that cause inherits the credibility of the correction. Attention holds through the gap between the denial and its replacement.
techniques.lands_when: The reader already has a name for what is going wrong, so there is something specific to take off the table.; The cause being dismissed is the one the audience would say out loud first.; The replacement cause points at something the offer or argument can actually reach.; The swap is stated in a line or two, in ordinary words, rather than argued at length.
techniques.dilutes_when: The dismissed cause is one nobody actually believed, so the correction has nothing to push against.; The run of denials gets long enough that every plausible cause is ruled out and the claim starts to sound impossible.; The replacement stays so vague that the reader cannot picture it or check it.; The copy denies something the reader can plainly see working, which reads as a lie rather than a cor…
